MEMPHIS, Tenn, March 9.-This morn
ing's light disclosed the dead bodies of
the three negroes taken from Jail, rid
died with bullets and partly covered
with brush, and lying in an open lot
about mile and half from the heart
OF the city. The negroes had been
taken from jail by seventy-five masked
men this morning aud shot to death.
The names of the victims are Calvin
Mcdowell, William Stuart and Theodore
Moss.


The crime for which this summary
vengeance was wreaked upon them was
the ambushing and shooting down Sat-
urday night OF four deputy sheritfs, in
the locality known as 1.-THE curve"
while the officers were looking for
negro for whose arrest they had war
rant.


About O'Clock this morning seventy
five men, all wearing masks, appeared
suddenly on Front street, near the Jail.
By a ruse three men obtained entrance
to the Jail yard and overpowered Watch
man O'Donnell. whom they bound and
gagged. The others were then admitted
and search for the negroes was begun.
A guard in the meantime had been put
over the watchman. There were twenty
seven negroes there, all under arrest for
completely in Saturday nights affair,
and it was no easy task to distinguish
the three negroes wanted. They went
from cell to cell, the thoroughly alarmed
inmates coming to the doors and unwit-
tingly aiding them in the search. Alice
| .Inn vi ho ,,oscn and hor
cell in the upper tier peered down on
the strange and silent crowd. Moss, a
mail carrier, the first man identified,
| was taken from his cell and bound and
gagged, and soon after Mcdonald and
| Stuart were found and taken care of in
| the same way.


The captives being ready, they were
| dragged, pushed and hurried out of Jail.
In a few minutes the suburbs of the city
were reached, and in an open field near
| Wolf river the negroes met their doom.
A shot from a revolver crashed through
the cheek of Moss. This was a signal
| for the work. A terrible volley was
poured in upon the shivering negroes,
who instantly fell dead. The bodies
presented horrible sight. McDowell's 8
jaw was entirely shot away, and back OF
| his right ear WAS hole large enough to
admit a mars fist. His right hand,
too, was half blown off. Stuart was shot
in the mouth and twice in the back of
the head, and his body was riddled with
buckshot. Moss had an ear shot off and
several holes in the forehead. The mob
turned about after its horrible work,
and after coming toward town scattered
and disappeared.


The bodies OF the dead negroes were
brought to Walsh's Undertaking estab-
lishment this morning. In less than
fifteen minutes the place wassurrounded
by about twenty negroes, all afraid to
talk, however, on account OF the prox-
unity of the whites. An inquest was
held at 10 O'Clock and the bodies were
sent to their homes at ''the curve"


At 10:30 this morning word reached
this city that negroes were assembling
in large numbers at ''the curve" and
Judge Dubose Immediately equipped
ESQ men with Winchesters, and they
lave left the city for that locality.

The consular bureau Of the State Department
anticipates vigorous objection from the differ
ent American consular officers whose salaries
have been reduced by the appropriation bill
for the fiscal year 1898. Many have already
forwarded animated protests to the department.
These came from consulates in Germany,
France, Venezuela, England, Scotland. Italy,
Sweden, Canada and other points. The con-
suls say it will be impossible for them TO per-
form the duties required with the money appro-
priated. Tho only recourse they have,
however, is to resign. State Department
officials say the reduction viii stop the issuing
Of consular reports, which have proven more
or less valuable to the country. The department.
frequently receives requests from chambers Of
commerce, as well as from individuals, for in
formation on certain industries abroad These
requests are sent to the consular officers for re-
ply. The answers are embodied in pamphlet
issued by the State Department and circulsted
throughout the United States.

PORTLAND, Ore, Oct. 12.-Miss Brudel
Morden, aged IS, was shot and probably
mortally wounded near her home at
Mount Tabor Villa, tonight, by Brudoth
Wolf, aged 81. For some time Wolf
had been keeping company with Miss
Morden, but she had apparently grown
tired of his attentions. Abouth s
O'Clock tonight Wolf met Miss Morden
and her sister in the road. He asked
Brndel to take walk with him, and
when she refused, he seized her by the
hand, and, drawing revolver, shot her

penetrated the girls lung, and that
there is little hope of her recovery.

SAN DIEGO, April 26.-The United
States cruiser Boston arrived here today.
While in Mexican waters some time ago
the Boston received orders from the
navy department to search the Revilla
Giodo islands for shipwrecked sailors
supposed to have been lost somewhere
in that group. The islands are off MAJ
allan on the coast of Mexico. 1t was
near them that last September the brig
Tahiti was found floating bottom side
up, and it was supposed that some of
the sailors might have made landing
upon the islands. The Tahiti was said
to have been agenuine pirate and elaver,
and was loaded down with natives from
the South Sea islands, who were being
taken. to the weet coast of Mexico to
work in the sugar and coffee plantations.
The crew and slaves were all lost. The
Boston made thorough search of these
islands, but found no trace of any living
human beings. The Boston will remain
here till Saturday and then proceed to
San Francisco.

An Eastern free-trade paper says:


England under free trade supplies her own
home market with manufaet ured goods and
articles much more fully than our manufacture
supply this market after nearly hundred
years Of protection.


When England established free trade it
had almost complete possession Of its own
home market. When thu United States
adopted a protective policy we bought al
most everything from abroad. The hand
loom made about all the cloth that was
made in the country. Under free trade
England has partially lost her home mar
ket, while under a protective policy the
United States has very largely taken pos
session of lis markets. In other words
under free trade England has lost much Of
what she possessed, while under a protec-
tive policy the United States acquired much
of what ii did not possess. The same
journal says:


Under free trade England is the greatest COM
mercial nation 10 the world while under high
tariff our flag has almost disappeared from the
seas.


Our contemporary confounds foreign COM
MERGE with the ocean carrying trade. they
are as distinct industries AS selling goods
and delivering them. The carrying trade is
done by the nation that will do it at the
lowest charge. Cheap labor is one of the
factors 10 the problem. A nation may do
large carrying trade and but little foreign
commerce. or it may have a large foreign
commerce and do but small ocean carry
ing trade. Cheap coal, cheap iron and
cheap labor have enabled England to do the
carrying trade at less cost than other
nations could do it.

communication inviting the House to at
tend the funeral ceremonies of the late

priation of $4,000 for detecting persons
guilty of violation of the internal revenue

mense river and harbor bill. He indorsed

replied, predicting the failure of the sub
treasury scheme and downfall Of the ALI
ance party. Simpson denied that the
leaders of the Alliance had adj
vised the farmers to hold the
grain, and said the members of
the Republican party were the only
persons who advised the course in aues-
ton. Simpson said that unless the
farmers were given the same equality as
was given the gold and silver miners and
bondholders they would know the reason
why after the next election. Watson of
Georgia and Davis of Kansas advocated
the sub-treasury system. The clause for
the recoinage, reissue and transportation
of minor coins having been reached, Tracy
of New York made a point OF order against
it, as he did also against free silver
amendment offered by Bartine of Nevada.
Both points went over for the present
without decision. The committee then
rose and the House adjourned.

A Gratifying Improvement in Fruit,

SACRAMENTO, May 14.-The monthly
crop report Of the State Agricultural
society shows a gratifying improvement
in fruits, grapes and grain. The late
rains did thousands of dollars worth Of
good in the San Joaquin valley and in
Monterey and San Luis Obispo counties.
Frost somewhat shortened the berry
crop and prunes. Most all other crops
will make an average yield. Late rains
and high winds have injured beans in
Santa Barbara and Ventura counties,
and much ground will require replant-
ing.


The past weeks weather conditions,
rainfall, temperature and sunshine,
have advanced the crop condition most
favorably. and the cool weather pre-
vented rust from taking an injurious
hold upon the great wheat belt Of Cali
fornia.

Jessie Dunbar, an Alameda street girl,

ing to the court that Officer Inns had

Three brothers, all humpbacked and all

My husband is very jealous" said she

Follow me if you value your lives"


She ordered the servant not to open the

veyed the brothers down the stairs and
locked them in the cellar.


Her husband sc0lded for being kept out

Il, H. IL ~
popped the body into the sack, took it to the

Are these your tricks, MASTER" said he.

ms time he returned in triumph, for the

A San Francisco paper of Friday con-
tains special dispatch from Pomona as
follows:


Every one at the little village of Ell
Monte, west of Pomona valley, is talk
ing about very singular occurrence
near that place last night and the mys-
terry that envelops the affair. Some
time between and 2 O'Clock this morn.
ing Eli w. Knapp, a dignifed and very
modest middle-aged man, living on the
main road between Pomona and Los
Angeles, was aroused from his slum bers
by some one at his front door. Before
he opened the door he heard woman q
voice. She was asking to be let into
the house for protection.


When Mr.. Knapp had dressed and
stepped out upon his porch he was al
most paralyzed to see standing before
him, in full blaze of his lamp, hand
some young woman, about five feet six
inches in height, with hardly any
clothing on her body. Her long hair
hung dsheveled about her neck and
her face was marked with tears, while
her plump arms and neck were slightly
bruised.


When Farmer Knapp could realize
that he was awake and not dreaming,
he called the young woman into the
house and Mrs. Knapp gave her some
clothing. 1t was then seen that the
strange woman was person of means.
She wore several solitaire diamond
rings, and her face and conversation
bore evidences of refinement. She said
she was 27 years old, but refused to say
who she was or how she came there,
except that she had been out driving
with a party of ladies and gentlemen
from Los Angeles. On the way back to
the city the men, who had become in
toxicated, had misued and insulted her.
She had a scuffle in the road with them.
and, while attempting to flee, all of her
clothing was torn away from her. She
escaped and walked over two miles in
the dark and cold to Farmer Knapp's
house.


The Knapps built fire in the stove
and were preparing meal for their
guest when she stealthily fled from the
house and got away in the dark. This
morning there were marks of hard
scuffle on the road and carriage tracks,
but all that remained of the garments
were very small bits OF the dress and
pieces of embroidery from undercloth-
ing. No one is able TO give any informa-
tion about the woman.

Detective Walter Auble left last even
ing for San Francisco to bring back to
Los Angeles two burglars, Charles
Wagon and John Loper, who have been
arrested by Chief Crowley and his force.
On Friday, April 1st, Judge Bicknell, at
his house, No. 227 South Broadway,
found the two men, who were tramps,
nosing about the premises. They told
the Judge that they were looking for
work, and the proprietor of the place,
who was preparing to move his house,
engaged them to tear up the brick of
walk in his back yard. In the mean
time, he gave them permission to sleep
in an outhouse in the rear of his place.


On the next day, Saturday, the two
men overheard the Judge saying that he
would take his family to Monrovia, and
they made their plans accordingly. AS
soon as the family had gone, Wagon and
Loper broke open the back door and
lifted b second door from it's hinges.
They then obtained an entrance to the
building and rifed all the dressing cases
and drawers in the house. They secured
lot Of plunder, including gold watch
and chain and valuable Knight Tenn
plar charm, on the back of which was
engraved the name 81. j. Reynolds"


After the burglars had completed
their work they found their way to
Judge BicknelPs wine cellar, and also
discovered box of Perfecto cigars.
They took several bottles of fizz and
the hsvanas to the judges parlor, made
themselves comfortable, and enjoyed
themselves to their taste. A lady Of the
neighborhood, at about 6 O'Clock that
day, called at the Bicknell house, and
walked to the back door. She received
no answer to her knock, and finding the
doors open, walked into the house.
She was suSprised to find no one pres
ent, and was still more surprised, when
she opened the parlor door, to find two
men having blowout among the biic-
a-brac. Wagon, when the lady ar
rived, at once politely arose and
explained that he and his partner had
been hired to take down the pictures
and prepare them for transportation.
This seemed satisfactory and the caller
left.


When Judge Bicknell and his family
returned. they found, of course, that the
house had been robbed. Notice was at
once given to the police authorities, and
a description OF the two tramps was
added. The description was at once
spread broadcast among the coast towns
and elsewhere, and yesterday Chief
Glass was delighted with the informa-
ton that the two thieves had been
in San Francisco. Detective Auble and
his prisoners will probably arrive here
on Tuesday.

LONDON. Dec. 3.-The German LLOYD
steamer Spree, reported overdue yesterday.
arrived at Queenstown to-day in tow of the
British steamer Lake Huron.


The main shaft of the Spree was broken
early on the morning of November 26 and
before the engines could be stopped the
broken shaft had pounded out portion of
the stern OF the steamer, and part of the
machinery went through the bottom under
the second cabin. which immediately filed
with water. The passengers thought the
vessel was going to the bottom and rushed
on deck. For time q veritabie panic pre-
vailed. and the officers were helpless to
calm the terrerized passengers. The water
could be heard rushing through the hold in
the bottom, and In short time the vessel
began to settle. The widest confusion en-
sued. but when 1t was discovered that the
vessel was not Immediately going to the bot
tom semblance OF order was resumed.
Nevertheless the passengers were anxious,
and kept their life e-preservers close at hand.


The boat crews were piped to their sta
tlons aud everything was placed In readi-
ness for the abandonment of the vessel. 1t
was soon found, however. that the water
tight bulkheads were answering the pur-
pose for which they had been constructed,





compartments beneath the second cabin
very little was reaching the other parts OF
the vessel.


When the accident occurred the Spree
was about 1000 miles from Queenstown.
Two anxious days passed and then the
Lake Huron took the disabled vessel in
tow. There were 2S3 passengers on board,
among them being General Howard,
U. S. a.; Mrs. Adelaide Howard and
child. Dwight L. Moody. the evangelist;
Mrs. Lewis Braeh and family of Milwau-
kee, DR.. Sidney Gum Of Chicago and many
others.


seeond-class passenger named Paul
Ke!son was so badly frightened after the
accident that he jumped overheard and was
drowned. The other passengers are all
well. Some of the passengers and por-
uon of the Spree's mail will be forwarded
by the Etruria tomorrow and the others by
the North German Lloyd steamer Havel,
which leaves Bremen tomorrow for
Queenstown to embark them.


Captain Milligerode. in an interview, SAYS
he never before had such an eyeu,ful
voyage. The weather was favorable and
splendid progress was made until the acei-
dent occurred. Immediately after the crash
the captain and crew took strong measures
to prevent the water entering other than
the damaged compartments.


After strenuous efforts these measures
were crowned with success, and at o'clock
In the afternoon, seven hours after the
accident, the captain was able TO announce
10 his passengers that the water was under
control and would undoubtedly be confined
TO the damaged compartment.


Grave fears still existed of serious conss-
Gueuees should bad weather be experienced.


Throughout Saturday and Sunday the
crew worked energetically and secured the
bulkheads in such manner that the ves-
sci was considered safe. The vessel drlfted
southwark. and then the wind changed and

There were the widest scenes OF Joy and
emotion when the Lake Huron was sighted

a heavy sea was running and 1t was
necessary to wait for daylight before line

was successfully accomplished, and then,
amid rousing cheers from the passengers.
the two ships got under way at o'clock for

was reached without further incident.


Dwight Moody presided at prayer meet
meeting on Sunday, and all the passenger
petitioned the Almighty to preserve them.


Thanksgiving service were held aboard

nest of tramps. loafers and drunks. The

though endowed with wings. - strong
north wind was blowing and the block on

wooden buildings were in the midst of
sea OF flame within forty minutes after the
alarm was sounded. To the south it
caught Mrs. Bsrrett's residence and to
the west the livery barn of +. McClintic.
So fierce was the heat from the flames that
the fire made its way back against the
wind, taking Reinhart's store, Noftsger's
store and dwelling. the Long building and
the store building of John Mairs. A: the
Odd Fellows hall and the courthouse, pro-
tected by intervening vacant spaces and
North street, it's progress was stopped.
The iron roof Of the Long building which
smothered the fire below when it fell, saved
the courthouse and Odd Fellows hall.


At this iuncture the Centralia steamer
arrived, after a delay of nearly IN hour
and half. The boys from above, rs they
raced down from the train, were greeted
with prolonged cheers, but they had come
too late to render assistance. The fire was
burned out.


The area burned comprised the heart of
the old business section oil Chehalis, and
formerly constituted the center OF town.

right of-way, on Front street.

KANSAS CITY, Aug. 2l.-The Journals

10:30 last night was held up and the
Wells-Fargo express car robbed by four
masked men near Augusta, Butler county,
about midnight. Before 9 o'clock this
morning the outlaws were captured, with
part of their booty.


As the train slowed at the crossing, one
mile east of Augusta. two masked men
mounted the locomotive and ordered the
engineer and fireman to stop the train.
This was done, and two other members of
the gang uncoupled the express car.
The engineer was then compelled
to pull out mile distant with
the express car. The highwaymen
demanded admittance, and commenced
shooting through the sides. The express
messenger and baggage men soon gave in.
Express Messenger Stiff was forced to open
the safe, and the robbers got between ten
and twenty packages of money. The out
laws did not attempt to rob the passengers,
and the latter knew nothing of the robbery
till it was over. The amount of money Sc
cured probably did not exceed $S,O00 but
the amount cannot be definitely ascer-
tained.


The robbery was committed by four
farmers living in the vicinity of Douglas,
Butler county, and it seems it was antici-
pated. for as soon as the sheriff heard of
the affair he pounced upon the outlaws.

Stevenson, the psymaster of the phos-

carrier, left Hernandon in a wagon.
About half way between the station and
the phosphate mine, the conveyance
was found, shortly after 6 O'Clock last

brains were blown out. Payne was in

but the bodies were still warm. Eight
cen hundred dollars which Stevenson
had in his possession were not secured
by the murderers, but two valises
which the unfortunate men had
,put into the wagon were missing.

covered a white man saw two negroes
near the place. He has given an accu-
rate description of each. Their clothes
indicated that they were phosphate
miners. One body had five and the
other six pistol shots in it. The greatest
excitement prevails, and searching
parties are being organized. The mana
ger of the phosphate company offers a
large reward for the capture of the
murderers. dead or alive.

Down Only When Shot.


Chris Ortholf the genial William street
barber, whose ingenious mind keeps him
busy when away from his keen edged
razors working up some curious con-
trivance, and Peter Keller had novel
and thrilling experience while expert
menting with a large balloon Tuesday
afternoon. For some time Chris has been
working upon balloon designed to carry
o small basket, in which he could sail
over sthe meadows in duck season and
from his aerial perch shoot the game as
it passed over the high grass.


Accompanied by James Taft, Peter
Keller and Joe McNulty, Chris carried
his aerial contrivance to point on the
river road near the Jersey City water
works. The balloon was tied down to
stakes driven in the earth, and after
being filed with hot air gracefully rose
to distance of several feet above the
ground, moving with an undulating mo-
tion in the strong breeze blowing across
the river.


TWAS intended that the balloon should
rise to certain height, and for this pur-
pose long rope had been attached to
the basket with one end fastened to a
tree. While Chris and Keller were hold
ing the basket preparatory to attaching
the rope, a strong wind caught the bal
loon, causing the ropes holding it down
to break. Before the men could loosen
their hold upon the basket the balloon
shot up through the air with lightning
rapidity, carrying Chris and Keller with
it. The former attempted to get into
the basket in order to reach the check
line and allow the air to escape, but the
smallness of the wicker box and it's sway
ing motion frustrated his efforts.


The balloon rose to distance of about
thirty feet with the men clinging to the
sides Of the basket. 1t then moved out
over the river and again began to rise
gradually.


AS the position of the men was becom-
ing serious, their companions below be-
came alarmed. Seeing that it was i'm
possible for him to direct his airship,
Chris called to Taft and McNulty to
pierce the balloon with shots from the
rifles which had been carried over by
the men. Chris, knowing that the un-
erring aim of both McNulty and Taft,
who are excellent marksmen, made him
secure from receiving charge from
one of the rifles, decided it was the best
course to pursue. Keller, however, be-
came alarmed when the shots began to
strike above his head, and was about to
take the risk Of dropping fifty feet into
the river than run the chances Of being
shot, when he was prevailed upon to re-
tain his hold.


In short time the aim of the men be-
low began to tell upon the balloon, and
the perforations made in the side Of the
airship let out the air, causing it grad
ually to sink. When within twenty feet
of the water a shot from one of the rifles
struck one of Keller's fingers, and be-
coming excited he loosed his hold upon
the basket and dropped into the river.
The balloon was now sinking rapidly,
and when the basket was within few
feet of the surface of the water Chris
dropped into the river to aid Keller,
who was struggling to keep afoat.


In the meantime the men upon the
shore had manned a boat and were pull
ing with all their might toward the men
in the water. Chris managed to keep
his companion above water until the
boat was alongside, and both men were
soon dragged aboard The balloon was
also taken aboard, and although thor
oughly soaked was not seriously dam
aged. d.-Belleville Press.

One morning little Bel was sent by her
mamma to the "button store" to match
a spool of silk. She had often been
trusted on such errands, though only
four years old, and very proud she used
to feel as she trudged along, helping
mamma"


''Be sure and get just that shade of
blue, and come right back, little daugh-
ter" said mamma as she kissed her
goodby.


Yes, ma'am," was the sturdy answer


Now ON the way to the button store
there was fruit stand, and Bel often
used to look at it with longing eyes,
This morning she saw something she
had not seen for a long time-great,
beautiful red bananas. If Bel liked any
thing in the world it was banana. She
wondered how much they would cost
Then she thought she would ask. Five
cents" Why, she had just five cents in
her fat fingers that very minute! Before
you could think she hadn't five cents at
all, but had the banana instead.

saying:


MY mother wants spool of silk like

The lady smiled down at the mite,

Flank you" said Bel. She never for

New YORK, May 16.-A heavy weight
glove contest between Joe Lannon and
George Godfrey drew large crowd to
the Coney Island Athletic club tonight.
Lannon tipped the scales at 175 and
Godfrey at 1856. Godfrey was the first
to land, which he did hard with both
right and left. He landed many good
blows before Lannon got down to work,
but when the latter did commence to
fight, he got in some left-handed jabs
and several hard right-handed swinging
blows. In the sacond and third both
men fought in vicious manner, and a
number of telling blows were struck.
Lannon was knocked down in the third
but was quickly up again.


The fourth round was the fercest and
most exciting in the fight, and settled
the battle. Lannon directed all his
blows for Godfrey's stomach, while the
colored man played for Lannon's head
entirely. He kept jabbing him straight
in the face with his left, and swinging
his right back of Lannon's ear until he
had him 90 groggy he could scarcely
stand. Lannon swung vicious right,
but it fell short of it's mark. Before he
could recover, Godfrey landed right
handed uppercut which sent Lannon
staggering across the stage, and another
from the shoulder with his left, knocked
him down and almost out.


As soon as he got up, Godfrey went at
him again, hammer and tongs, Lannon
growing weaker every second. Both
were go much excited that neither
seemed to hear the gong at the call of
time, and went right on fighting. Both
Of them delivered foul blows, but Lam
mons had little steam in them, while
three of Godfrey's terrific swings almost
put Lannon out. The seconds of both
men yelled foul" and the referee, AL
Smith, grabbed Godfrey and dragged
him away from Lannon. The entire
crowd shouted foul" end the widest
excitement prevailed. The referee
turned deaf ear to all the appeals of
Lannon's friends, and ordered the men
to 90 on fighting.


At the call of time for the fifth round,
Godfrey responded, but Lannon refused
to get up, whereupon the referee
awarded the victory to Godfrey. Lam
non was very much exhausted and could
hardly have lasted another round.

LINCOLN, Neb., March 31.-Unconfrmed
reports have reached this city that a
cyclone struck the town of Nelson. wreck
ing it badly. Edgar, in Clay county, is
also said to be damaged. The depot was
blown down and two men killed. The

Specials from Wahoo and Norfolk tell of

houses being blown down, but no serious
damage resulting. In this locality the
wind has blown gale all the afternoon
and evening, followed by heavy rain.


OMAHA, March 81 "A special to the Bee
from Nelson says: A terrible cyclone
struck Nelson this evening. 1t came from
the southwest. and could be seen at least
ten minutes before it struck the town.
1t was preceded by a terrific hail
storm, lasting several minutes, after
which came storm which proved
the worst and most destructive
that ever visited this section of Nebraska.
The storm struck the town with terrible
force at SIS. Many rushed to cellars and
stores for safety The damage has been
estimated at 100000. The First, Ma
tional bank was unroofed, the opera
house block unroofed and badly
damaged; the Union block unroofed
and the southwest end torn out; the Ar
lington hotel unroofed, and a new school
house costing $4,000 almost destroyed.
The Presbyterian church was badly
wrecked, and 4 large number of residences
completely wrecked, nothing being left
except the cellars and foundations. Half
of house. that of Henry L.
Pope, was carried along in the track
of the storm nearly an eighth of a
mile, with the contents and Mrs. Pope and
two children. Fortunately, however, the
family escaped uninjured. Mrs. Mary
Brayman, assistant principal of the Nell
son High school, was seriously hurt, hay
ing leg and several ribs broken. Mrs.
John Eaton was also seriously injured.
Most of the buildings we're insured only
against fire, and the loss is almost total.
Nothing has yet been learned as to the
damage done in the surrounding country.

taking rooms of Garrett q Sampson,

foot shark was part of their catch. At first

men 10 haul him close up to the boat. Carlo

Hit in the body OF the monster. which at

dashed the water into foam and nearly up
Set the beat several times. Again and

About a year ago G. w. Strickland, a
young farmer, living about six miles
southwest of Paris, fell in love with Miss
Ida Porter, charming young lady of the
same neighborhood. The lady's relatives
objected but the young folks resolved to
elope. Mr.. Strickland got license, but
the issuance of the license was published
in the papers and before chance came
to use it the relatives of the lady saw it
and sent her away to Missouri.


A few weeks ago she came back. Her
relatives thought the affair was ended.
but the young folks stillloved each other.
There were some private negotiations of
which her relatives did not know An
other license was procured, but the fact
was not published in the papers. The
same minister was engaged again. Miss
Ida Porter, who did not usually pick cot
ton, suddenly became very industriously
inclined, and concluded to help pick out
the crop. She went into the field and
began work. Pretty soonher big brother,
not suspecting anything, went to the gin
with load of cotton, and about the

Capt. George Porter bought the Lou
in 1887 and used her for trading down
south. After while the Mexican gov
ernment, being suspicious that the Lou
was engaged in smuggling, chartered the
Carlos Pacheco and captured the vessel
in Mexican water. Captain Porter and
his crew were placed on board the Pa

into Rosalia bay. In the course of the
night the Americans escaped from the
Pacheco in row boat and boarded the
Lou. The Mexican officials were taken
completely by surprise. At the point of
revolvers they readily consented to va

vessel. Captain Porter and his men cut
the tow line and when the sun burst
forth in the morning the Lou was miles

A year later the Lou was the means of

provisions and without means of secur

Porter came along one day in the Lou

SANTA BARBARA, March 26.


The English flagship Warspite, long
looked for in this port, arrived about
dusk Saturday night, and remained
throughout Sunday and until about
O'Clock today.


The vessels movements we're kept a
profound secret, yet we learned that
leaving here, the Warspite will continue
direct to Esquimault, where further
orders will await her. Nothing could be
learned regarding the Bering sea, the
off GERS being adverse to saying any
thing whatever relating thereto. The
boats armament embraces two nine
inch guns, four eight-inch, four three
inch and two rapid firing boarding guns.
She is about the size of the Charleston,
yet she does not appear 20 be as formid-
able warship in any particular.

ports and from France.

apprehension, and many of the weathier

be issued by the authorities informing the
people OF the best method to live to avoid
the disease. Ali arrivals at this port from

express was just rounding the curve when

OF his visit here is to secure medical
aid for the unfortunate victims. The
fail festivals opened in Arteaga
this week, the feature of which
were bull fights. The great event
of the week was postponed I'm til yester-
day, when four wild bulls were turned

animals were turned into the arena. After

animal stampeded the others, and they

made for the protection of spectators.

Many odd and amusing stories are
told of the clever French critic, Jules
Janin, and his friends. None is more
pleasing or more to their credit than
one in which Janin, Theodore Burette,
the historian, and Leon Satayes, the
composer, author and critic, figured.
One of Janin's best friends was an old
aunt, who sent him to school when he
was boy, kept house for him and took
good care of him when he, Young
man, was making his reputation. but
not much money, in literature.


1t was perhaps in memory of her that
he made a protege of poor old woman
whom he noticed one day in the street.
He placed her in home for aged per-
sons, and until her death years after
ward was her thoughtful and generous
friend. The good woman was verv ill
once, and when she was convalescing
she said:


IL want to go and call on M. Janin. I
must see him once more before die"


One Of the women of the institution
went with her. Janin was living then
in the top of house which commanded
q beautiful view of the garden of the
Luxembourg. His "garret'' was filled
with books and pictures, but like any
other garret it was reached by climbing
great many stairs Slowly and pain
fully the old woman toiled up the long
flights. She had to sit down often to
rest. 1t took her nearly two hours to
reach the top. Janin was breakfasting
with Theodore Burette.


He received her with great cordiality
and affection, and the three had happy
breakfast. The two men devoted them
selves to entertaining her. They in
Quired all about the home, the rules, the
diversions, the food, her recent illness,
and listened with genial interest to ali
she had to say. She said goodby, and
they made ready to escort her down
stairs.


"We will return your visit soon," they
said, and placing themselves on either
side of her they began to descend the
stairs. But the effort and excitement
had been too much for the feeble old
lady. Her limbs failed her and she
could not take step.


just then Satayes appeared on the
scene. "We must carry her down." he
said. So they placed her comfortably
in an armchair. Janin and Burette,
who were small men, took the back,
Satayes took the front, and they went
down fight after flight of the many
storied house breathless but cheerful.


swell, my good woman" gasped Sa.
tayes, 81 don't know of any queen who
has carriage like yours"


The three literary workers were hardly
In training for their achievement, but
they placed her safe and sound on the
sidewalk, and saw her go away with her
attendant, her old heart deeply touched
and pleased with the attentions she had
received.-Youth's Companion.

While making the balloon ascension and
parachute jump at Madison street park
yesterday afternoon Hazel Keyes, the lady
aeronaut, was injured internally and now
lies at the Pavilion in serious condition.
Professor J. J. Romig, who joins with her
in the performance. was alsOihurt, but not
seriously.


The balloon is inflated just south of the
ball grounds, within q lot inclosed by
picket fence. When it was released yester-
day it did not go straight up,
but was blown toward the lake.
Professor Romig saw that it was not
high enough to take the balloonists over
the sharp fence safely and made running
jump just before the fence was reached.
Fortune favored him; the balloon gave
him quick jerk and over he went. but in
doing 50 struck a man under the chin,
knocking him out.


Hazel Keyes did not fare so well. She
was swept against the fence, striking at
point near the diaphragm. As the bal
loon swept along she was dragged over
the fence, and carried up into the air.


So quickly did the whole affair take
place that only few persons noticed
that she was injured. With wonderful
nerve. she hung to the balloon and when
it was over the lake, cut herself loose and
sailed gently downward. She struck the
water a short distance northeast of the
wharf and was Immediately picked up by
boat which was in waiting. Even then
she remained calm, though she told her
attendants that she was injured. She was
taken quietly to a room in the Madison
street power-house and DR.. Hilton sent
for. Before he arrived she fell into an
epileptic fit. frothed at the mouth, talked
incoherently and became insensible. DR..
Hilton arrived as soon as posi-
bic and, upon examination, found
that she was in a very precarious condi-
ton. Her left ankle was sprained and the
toes of the foot crushed painfully, the
right leg, especially above the knee, was
battered and bruised. The most danger
our injury. however. was that in the body,
just below the chest. She is en- ceinte
and the exact effect the internal injuries
will have cannot be told. Late last night
she was resting easily under opiates and
the doctor was in hopes that she would
escape serious results.


The patient was to have left the city
within few days to fill an engagement at
Napa, Cal, but this accident will cause
postponement of her engagement. A fact
not generally known is that Miss Keyes
was at one time resident of Seattle.

SAN Francisco, Dec 30.-A remarkable
scene was witnessed in Superior Judge
Hebbard's court room this morning dur
ing the trial of suit of the executors
of the Mervyn Donahue estate against
the Hotel San Rafael corporation. Some
time ago the directors of the corporation
were fined $500 for contemptfo disobey-
ing an injunction Of the court, but the
execution thereon had not yet been
issued. This morning Attorney Charles
Hanlon, who represents the plaintiffs,
entered his bill of costs. which, on mo-
tion OF ex-Superior Judge O. P. Evans,
counsel for the defendants, Judge Heb
bard ordered stricken out. Evans
then asked a stay of execution
in the matter of the $500 fine.
This greatly astonished Hanlon, who
asked if Evans had not promised him
that if the bill of costs were not pressed
Evans clients would pay the fine.
Evans denied having go stated, where
upon Hanlon called him liar. The ex-
Judge retaliated by shooting his right
fist into Hanlon's face, and in minute
the two attorneys were hammering each
other about the court room. BaiiiH
O'Neill was ordered to separate them,
but before he could do SO Evans had
knocked Hanlon down. When order
was finally restored Judge Hebbard
summarily fined. the combatants $500
each and ordered them imprisoned FIVE
days in the county Jail.


Subsequently the two attorneys apol-
ogized to the court, Hanlon stating
at the same time that he had not been
struck by Evans's blows, and that he
had no recollection of having called the
latter liar. They asked that the order
committing them to Jail be vacated
which Judge Hebbard finally consented
to, but insisted that the fine should be
paid. The two attorneys drew their
checks for the amount, and addressing
each other in a friendly fashion, left
the courtroom together.


1t was stated when order was restored
that Hsnlon had not been knocked
down by Judge Evans, but had Stun
bled and fell.

ing light disclosed the dead bodies of three

names of the men are Calvin Mcdowell,
William Stewart and Theodore Moss.
The crime for which this sum-
mary vengeance was wreaked upon them
was the ambushing and shooting down on
Saturday night last of four deputy sheriffs
in the locality of the territory known as
THE Curve" while the officers were look
ing for negro for whose arrest they
had warrant. About O'Clock
this morning seventy-five men. all wearing
masks, appeared suddenly on Front street.
near the jail. By ruse three men
obtained entrance to the Jail yard and
overpowered the Waterman. whom
they bound and gagged. The others
were then admitted and the search for
the negroes began, guard in the mean
time having been put over the Waterman.
There were twenty-seven negroes there,



day nights affair." and it was not an easy
task to distinguish the three negroes
wanted. They went from cell to cell and
thoroughly aroused the inmates, who,
coming to the cell doors, unwittingly
aided them in the search.

her cell on the upper tier peered down on
the strange and silent crowd. Moss. the
IL, I
taken from his cell and bound. and soon

ellis jaw was entirely shot away and

ing. In less than fifteen minutes the
place was surrounded by about twenty

Behanzin commanded the Dahomeyans

fire with marvellous bravery.

ALFRED X. CALHOUN IN HOME AND COUNTRY
OF the camp, the march, the battle,


Let other soldiers sing;
Let them show our tatter'd banners,


While on high their hats they hing.
The saber, the old musket


Can everywhere be seen,
But there's nothing brings war days to mind
Like you-my old canteen.
A thousand friends who kissed you


Are gone forevermore;
Cried "Herev' to the mystic angel,


And crossd to the other shore.
You are rusty; you are batter'd;


Gone is your early sheen,
But the trumpet's blast can't thrill me
Like you-my old canteen.
They intended you for water


When they framed your rounded side,
Yet you kindly took to-coffee,


For your symPathies were wide;
Distilled peach and "commissary"


You have held with sober mien,
And you often furnished bourbon


On the night march-old canteen.
When comrades fell about me
You stuck closer to my side:
You brought comfort to the wounded,


VINO without you must have died;
Even gen'rals have praised you


When they tasted you unseen
And have wiped their boards and WHISPERED:
THAT'S bully old canteenl"
We've slept and marched together:


we've been empty, we've been full;
We've merry made DER stolen sweets,
With buttermilk been dull;
We've heard fierce oaths DER sore defeat,
And the foe in fight we've seen,
Then crippled, sore, but stout of heart,
Came home-my old canteen.
When comrades take me to the grave,
I'd have you brought there, too;
Pass from lip to lip In silence,


With my dead face In their view.
Then let them lay you on my heart,
And place us meath the green,
And say: "He was a soldier true:


He loved his old canteen"

WASHINGTON, Dec. 24.-The President
has called upon the executive departments
for all information in their possession rela-
tive to the freight coming into the United
States over the Canadian Pacific Railroad.
The unjust discrimination against the
United States railroads made by the law, or
rather by its construction. in favor OF the
Canadian Pacific by means of the consular
seal system has long been source of COM
plant at the Treasury Department. By
this Interpretation OF the law freight is
shipped from Canada to interior points In
the United States under the consular seal
system. A United States Consul certiiies
that the manifest is correct, and that lie
has sealed and closed the car, and that Ger
tifcaton carries the freight through with
out inspection, thus saving from one TO
two days delay aud the cost of rehandling
freights. When this law was passed this
class Of traffic was small. but gradually
the business has grown until Instead of
handling only Canadian goods in this way
the law has been perverted. and now more
goods having their origin in China and Ja-
pan are shipped over the Canadian Pacific
through the United States than goods made
in Canada. Furthermore, the Canadian Pa
cific has managed TO have duty of 10 per cen (
placed upon coffee or tea coming from tie
United States into Canada. while the same
articles come from other countries free
The effect of this has been to divert this
traffic from American ports. and 10 have
the coffee and tea come East over the Cana
dian Pacific from Vancouver, B. C.


These evidences of unfriendliness are re-
garded at the State Department as requiring
some drastic measures, and it is therefore
proposed to suspend the operation of said
section until Congress shall make proper
provision 10 stop the discrimination against
American railroads

Associated Press Dispatches


OMAHA. Neb., April 14.-The fight be-
tween the Boyd and Martin factions in
the Democratic state convention, con-
tinued all night before the committee
on credentials. After brief respite,
the struggle was renewed this morning.
and the convention kept waiting all the
morning by the failure of the creden-
tials committee to report. The dele.
gates from the various congressional
districts selected delegates to the Chi
cago convention. The majority OF these
are Boyd men and against instructing
for Cleveland.


1t was nearly noon when Chairman
Beatty called the convention to order.
The committee on credentials reported
in favor of seating the Boyd delegation
from Boyd, Cheyenne, Counning and
Hitchcock counties. The motion to
adopt the committee reports was
amended to seat the Martin delegates.
Then the final struggle for supremacy
began. County Attorney Mahoney
spoke in favor of the Martin faction /;
Charles Otfut presented Boyd's case.


A vote was then taken. The Boyd fac
ton was victorious, 300 to 81.


A resolution endorsing Cleveland and
instructing the delegates to the national
convention to vote for him was present.
ed. An amendment was presented elm
mating instructions. This was adopted
and the resolution as amended passed.


Governor Boyd was selected delegate
at-large by practically unanimous vote.
The other delegates are Tobias Castor,
Judge W. H.. Thompson and Milton
Doolittle.


The committee on resolutions then re-
ported, declaring steadfast adherence to
the Democratic platform of 1884 and
Cleveland's tariff policy; denouncing
the Mckinley law; favoring liberal pen
sions, and regulating railroad and tele-
graph rates by the state.


Congressman Bryan offered resolu-
tion favoring the free coinage of silver.
An uproar ensued. Congressman By
mum spoke in favor of the resolution,
supported by delegates from the western
portion OF the state, but the other prom
inent leaders Of the party were against
him. After hot debate lasting three
hours the roll was called, when Chair
man Beatty announced the defeat of the
resolution by 247 to 229. Pandemonium
then broke loose. The silver men made
a rush for the stage, and, mounting the
recorders table, shrieked that they
were beaten by fraud. Finally quiet
was restored and the result of the vote
verified.


After the selection of alternates to
the national convention, the convention
adjourned.

night, and all night the splendid rooms
were filled with guests and ablaZe with
light. After spending a full million for
his house the host did not stint his guests
in the matter of entertainment. The best
musicians, the best entertainers of every
kind, were paid princely sums for catering
to the pleasure of the Fishers guests.
Feasts and revelry were the serious bust
ness of all who were so lucky as to be in
yited there.


But the very gayety which made the
Fisher manor one of the most pleasant
spots in California was the cause of its
ruin. Wine, like all other good things,
was there in unlimited quantities. Mrs
Fisher soon contracted love for liquor
which nothing could hold in check. While
her husband was present she at first con-
trolled her awful desire, but when business
called him to London she threw aside all
reserve and all restraint and plunged into
the widest dissipation.


She was not a strong woman and it could
not last. One day her husband returned
and found her dying. Fisher watched over
her until she died in wild delirium, call
ing frantically for drink.


Broken hearted Fisher shut up the
house and lived alone. Losses came thick
and fast; his business in London failed and
he was unable to meet his bills. The resi-
dence was seized by the creditors and
Fisher returned to London drink COM
pleted his wreck, and he died, they say, in
an almshouse.


Then came the auction of the furniture
1t was all magnificent. Pieces were sold
for few hundreds which had cost twice
as many thousands. The place itself,
which had cost over q million of dollars,
was offered for sale at q third as much, but
found no purchasers.


Even then there was a rumor, vague dt
first, but soon grown into definite story,
that although Mrs. Fisher had left her
splendid residence forever her spirit was
loath to part with what had been its de.
light. Ghostly stories of woman in
white, who passed through the handsome
corridors holding to her breast a bunch of
violets were freely told. Many who visit
ed the magnificent chamber where Mrs
Fisher died averred that the odor of violets
in the room was almost overpowering, al
though there were no vioiets nearer than a
mile.


The creditors, despairing of ever selling
the place, hired person after person to live
in the basement and take care of the house.
They all left after a short stay, scared
away by the ghosts, people said. One old
sea captain alone lived there for over a
year, and the stories he told were fearful.
Finally he, too, left and died.


Then the trustees hired family named
Vertrang to keep the house. They had
been servants of the Fishers, and thought
they could stand the ghosts. One day two
years ago, however, a second tragedy was
enacted at the place. An artist climbed
into tree above the house and took poison.
His body lay there for two weeks before it
was found This of course gave rise to
even more stories of wraiths and spooks.
But Vertrang and his wife say that they
have never seen anything amiss about the
place. They still live in the basement, and
the fact that they have claim of 5000
upon the estate may have something to do
with their courage.

ran. Fay pursued his victim and en-

Sailors yarns have always been cele-
brated for their imaginative character.
Those of today, however, have no oppor-
tunity for favorable comparison with the
stories told by mariners of antiquity.
The latter were able to count upon an
inexhaustible public credulity, nothing
which they could possibly invip being
too monstrous or unusual fof belief.
Their tales presumably did much. TO
augment the fears of the sea which were
commonly entertained in those days,
giving birth to many of the myths Of
ocean. They told about the strange land
inhabitated by lotos eaters, who fed upon
the fruit of forgetfulness and lost all
memory of country and friends. Hey
ond was the terrible land of the one eyed
giants, called Cyclops, they said, while
elsewhere were to be found the strange
islands where the enchantresses Circe
and Calypso lived. These islands were
in the narrow western Mediterranean
and beyond was the Cimmerian land,
where the people lived in darkness al
ways, inhabiting gloomy caves.


There were the Sirens also, whose song
was death. They were condemned to
die when man should pass them with
outstopping. Ulysses accomplished this
by putting wax in his ears So they
were changed into rocks of Sorrento,
where they still exist terror to mari
ners. The Sirens typify the surf, whose
harmonious murnurs are often the death
music Of the sailor. In like manner the
Cyclops represent the Storm Fiend, as
their names show. Rrontes is the roll
Steropes the flash and Argis the white
ness of lightning.


Likewise the snaky Gordons are
thought to be figurative representations
of the white capped and angry waves
Not less to be feared were the dreadful
Symplegades-huge moving rocks which
were tabled to crush ships passing be
tween them. 1t has been surmised thai
the tradition respecting these rocks was
derived from the floating icebergs, which
during the glacial period must have
issued from the Black sea; but this seems
hardly likely.-W Washington Star

In the afternoon the mob rapidly COL

PHILADELPHIA, Oct. 30.-A serious fire
occurred on the river this morning in
the vici uity of Point Breeze. 1t was
caused by an explosion of oil which
leaked from the large pipes connecting
the oil refineries on each side of the
Point Breeze gas works. The escaped
oil worked down through the soil and
collected beneath the furnaces at the
pumping station in large quantity.
When ignited, it exploded with sufi-
cient force to break down the retaining
wall, and the whole volume of oil spread
in burning mass over the sur
face of the river. The ebb tide
and stiff breeze carried the blazing
mass down the river. Great excite
ment followed among shipping men.
Tugs were hastily summoned to tow
away the steamers and sailing vessels
lying about. After hard work the larg-
est vessels got to places Of safety. The
bark Felix and several lighters burned.
The bark Elena and one or two other
vessels lost their rigging. Several small
houses on the bank and 500 feet of
wharving were destroyed. The loss will
aggregate $135, 900.

Bay All Day md Then Drowned.


SAN Francisco, Dec. 1.-Two fishermen
were drowned yesterday near the Berkeley
shore while southeast gale was raging.
For two hours they chung to the bottom Of
a boat, and when help was close at hand
the tired men gave out and fell back into
the bay. The men were Augustine Faul-
cent, owner of the boat, and Luigi Norris,
his assistant. It was predicted on Tues
day afternoon tina. the storm had passed
and clear weather was to follow. Early in
the evening the two men started out to
fish for sea bass. They had not gone far
when the gale struck them and Faulceni
decided to put back. but the force of the
wind blew the sail out and nearly capsized
the boat. The boat was rocked about like
a chip and big seas poured into
her. The entire night passed and
the boat got no further than
Goat island. In the morning she was
overturned and the men were thrown into
the bay. They were both good swimmers
and managed to climb onto the bottom of
the boat. The waves washed over them
again and again, but-they chung to the
keel with desperation. Their clothing was
heavy with salt water and their fingers
were numbed with cold. They at last
could hang on no longer and slid from the
bottom OF the boat into the bay and were
drowned.


Antonio Mar;ino was also caught by the
gale and narrowly escaped with his life.
He went out on Saturday night, when the
storm came on. Sunday he was driven
ashore on Sheep island, and there he re-
NAMED until rescued yesterday. When
picked up he was more dead than alive. as
he had had nothing to eat for four days.

Body Lodged Between Logs. Terribly

stages of decomposition, which precluded
the possibility of Identification. 1t was
lodged between two logs, and the head
having been caught by knot, it was kept
from slipping away and being carried down
the stream. Every vestige of clothing
was gone and the only personal property
left was the boots, which the water and
rocks had failed to tear away. The flesh
was gone from the right arm and the face

come in contact with sharp rocks. The
man was large and weighed about $50
pounds. and his hair was probably dark.

of workingman.

remains were those of one of the men

OMAHA, April 1.-THE fight between the
Boyd and Martin factions in the Demo-
cratic state convention, continued all
night before the committee on credentials
After a brief respite the struggle was re-
newed in the committee this morning, and
the convention was kept waiting ali the
morning by the failure of the credentials
committee. Separate delegates from the
various congressional districts in the eau
Gus selected delegates to the Chicago con-
vention. The majority of these are Boyd
men and are against instructing for Cleve-
land


1t was nearly noon when Chairman
Beatty called the meeting to order. The
committee on credentials reported in favor
of seating the Boyd delegation from Doug
las, Cheyenne. Cutting and Hitchcock
counties. A motion to adopt the commit
tees report was amended to seat the Mar
tin delegations. Then the final struggle
for supremacy began. County Attorney
Mahoney spoke in favor of the Martin
faction and Charles Offut presented the
Boyd factions case.


A vote was then taken, and the Boyd
faction was victorious 800 to 81.


Resolutions indorsing Cleveland and in
structing the delegates to the national con-
vention to vote for him were presented.
An amendment was presented eliminating
the instructions. This was adopted, and
the resolution as amended was passed.
The convention ratified the nomination
for delegates made by the congressional
districts, and then proceeded to the selec-
tion of delegates at large. Governor Boyd
was elected to head the delegation
by practically unanimous vote. The
other delegates are Tobias Castor, Judge
w. HI. Thompson and Milton Doolittle.
The committee on resolutions then re-
ported, declaring stea6fast adherence to
the Democratic platform of 1884 and the
Cleveland tariff policy; denouncing the
Mckinley law, favoring liberal pensions
and the regulation ofthe railroad and tele-
graph rates by the state.


At the conclusion of the platform Con-
gresham Bryan offered resolution favor
ing the free coinage of silver and uproar
ensued. Congressman Bryan spoke in
favor of the resolution and was supported
by delegates from the eastern part of the
state, but the other prominent leaders of
the party were against him. After a
hot debate, lasting three hours. the
roll was called, when Chairman
Beatty announced defeat of the resolution
by 2f7 to 229. Pandemonium broke loose.
The silver men made rush for the stage,
and, mounting the recorders table.
shrleked that they were beaten by fraud.
Finally quiet was restored and the re-
suits verified. After the selection of alter
mates to the national convention the con-
vention adjourned.

SANTA Rosa, Oct. 2S.-Constable Barn.
hardt had an exciting chase after burglar
named Geiger this morning. Stolen prop
erty has been found in the possession of the
man, and Mr.. Barnhardt was returning
from the mountains with the prisoner,
when. crossing the bridge over the Sou0ma
Creek near Los Guilcos. Geiger sprang
from the buggy to the rail of the bridge and
down into the creek He was very dexter
Gus in his movements. and the constable
could not get chance 10 shoot. After half
an hours search the constable saw the
prisoner cross a field and took after him
with horse. When within FIVE rods of the
prisoner the latter jumped into the brush
along the creek bank. Barn hardt followed
and saw footprints at the bottom OF pool
twenty feet across and three feet deep, but
Geiger had completely disappeared. When
about to give up the search Barnhardt
noticed movement on the surface of the
water few feet away, and looking closer
saw the nose of the escaped man just above
the water. The prisoner was finally landed
safely in jail. Three charges are against

The Southern Pacific Company has again
shown its utter disregard for the public at
large and echoed the words of Vanderbilt.
This time 1t has given Oakland taste of its
contempt for its patrons, and the inhsbi-
tants of the Athens of the Pacific will no
doubt show their resentment at the earliest
opportunity.


On Saturday night there were at least 200
people shut out from the last boat across
the bay and they had to skirmish for lOdg-
ings as best they might.


THE CARS STOPPED.


About half-past IL o'clock fire broke out
on Market street, near Sixth, and the con-
sequence was that the cable system was
stopped The fire did not amount to much.
but the hose was stretched across the street
for half an hour or more, and the dummies
could not cross it. 1t was probably good
thing for the late crowd gong west, but it
operated very poorly for those who wanted
to reach the ferry.


AS usual on Saturday night there was a
large crowd over here from Oakland, and
some were visiting and others were at the
theater but all had timed themselves 10
catch the last boat, and just knew when to
take the last car going east. As soon as
the hose was removed from the street,
the cars were put in motion, and amid the
changing of bells they went rolling down
Market street. All along the line they were
hailed, but the gripmen had their orders
and the cars stopped for no one. From
dozen to sixteen dummies rolled up to the
depot one after another with men who were
fortunate enough to be alone.


ANGRY CITIZENS.


Many people who had tired of waiting
for the cars. not knowing what was the
matter started to walk 10 the ferry. The
majority of these arrived at the depot just
after the first car, and they surged in toward
the gate.


Among the number we're some If Oak
lands best people. who had come over in
theater parties. With wild rush ladies
and gentlemen scrambled into the building
and reached the gates just in time to hear
the loud gong claDg and see the portals
swing closed. Then followed a scene hard
TO describe. There were men with their
wives and daughters, young girls who had
never remained night away from home,
young men with awful cares suddenly
thrust upon them, and pandemOnium was
let loose The men demanded the opening
of the doors and crowd rushed forward TO
batter them down. The police struggled
through to the head Of the surging crowd
as the whistle Of the departing steamer
sounded the death Knell of the hopes of
those who were left behind. Had it not
been for the officers the walls would have
been torn down.


a GRAVE SITUATION.


i
expense Of remaining in the city over night
was not by any means the gTavest feature
of the position. What were the young
ladies 10 do and how we're they to explain
their absence from home? There were
anxious mothers on this side as we'll as in
Oakland, aud altogether it was a pretty
mess. There were weeping misses and
wrathy men, and curses strong and deep
were mingled with sObs soft and silent. 1t
was not time, however, to waste IN idle
mourning, and those who had friends on this
side or funds 10 put up at
hotel boarded the cars which were now
plentiful enough and went uptown. There
were many embarrassing incidents, too.
Some of the young Athenian gentlemen,
who had spent their weeks salary on the
charming Athenian maidens, were at their
wits end to provide a cover for the fair
ones they had spent the evening with and
dallied until the last moment. and the blue
canopy Of heaven had 10 do its best for
them. Bow these unfOrtunates managed is
a mystery, but there were some very broken
up couples crossing the bay yesterday morn
ing on the early boat.


Over in Oakland, however, there were
many who passed a sleepless night. not
knowing what had happened to the belated
ones, and all day yesterday there were ex-
plantations and explanations.


The end has not yet come. Among the
possibilities are divorces and breach of
promise suits and other calamities.

Inc police last evening raided the gam
ping rooms of the city, and made sixteen
arrests. The proprietors of the games
nVe In number-were first arrested and
tnen Chief Rogers detailed several squads
OF police to visit the gambling-hodses a
second time and arrest the dealers and
seize the tools. All those arrested gave
bail IN the sum of SIS each. making total
OF 81, % The value of the gambling par
aphernalia seized is about $500. The
gamblers will be given a trial Monday
afternoon in the municipal court before
Judge River.


The raid was entirely unexpected, and
was made very suddenly, every one being
taken by surprise. First the chief de-
tailed Dete tives Phillips, Cave and Cudi-
hee, Inspector Willard and Lieutenant
Sims to arrest the proprietors of any
games found running. Detective Phillips
went to the NJ. and n. house, on Washing
ton street, besween South Second and
Commercial, end arrested William Como
yer; Inspector Willard went % the Clancy
Burns house and arrested Frank
Clancy; Lieutenant Sims went to the
Beede games, in the Butler block, and ar
rested Charles Mullen; Detective Cudihee
went to the Horse shoe games and arrested
J. L. Griffin; Detective Cave went to the
Delcho rooms and found Ri hard Kelley
in charge. At police hendqu.. tiers the
men were booked upon charges of con-
Quoting gambling games, and each gave
bail in the sum of $50.


As soon as the five men had been booked
the chief again sent out a squad of men
with orders to revisit the gambling rooms,
and, if any games were found running, to
arrest the dealers and seize the geming
tools. Inspector Willard, accompanied by
Officer Powers, Immediately went to
Clancy & Burns saloon on Jackson street,
but they could not get upstairs, owing to
the fact that before their arrival the
players were notified by sentinel that
the police were coming and the mob
fed; they rushed down the stairs four
abreast and swept everything before them.
The officers could not force their way
against this human current, and before
they got to the top of the stairway the
gambling implements had all been hidden
away.


Captain Barck, Detective Phillips and
Officer Steppler went to the NJ. and n.
rooms. The games were all running and
in the rooms were about 200 men, includ-
ing spectators and players. As soon as
the alarm was given every one made o
rush for the door, but Officer Steppler
barred the way and told them they would
have to remain inside. The patrol wagon
was sent for and $3.50 worth of tools were
seized and sent to headquarters. While
the games were being closed the street in
front of the house was filled by an excited
crowd. When the dealers, "Pop" Dolan,
James Burns aud G. w. Griffin appeared
from the building in charge OF officers, the
crowd went wild.


The inclement weather had tendency
to drive pedestrians under cover, and at
that hours 80 o'clock-the gaming rooms
all over town were crowded. The news
soon spread that the games were being
raided, and the loungers in the saloons all
turned out to see the fun.


The patrol wagon was next sent to the
Horseshoe and the Beede gaming houses.
The alley leading to the two houses was
already crowded with men, but the patrol
wagon was driven down and the mob
parted. right and left. There must have
been 500 spectators, and there was great
excitement.


In the Beede house were nearly $50
players and they were kept in the rooms
by Lieutenant Sims and Officer Birdsall,
while the dealers, directed by Officer Eos
ter, packed up their chips and other gam
ing tools. The biggest crowd of all was in
the Horseshoe. In this place there must
have been at least 300 players; the rooms
were packed almost to suffocation. The
appearance of the officers created conster-
nation and many attempted to escape, but
they found all the exits guarded. The
tools were wrapped up and taken to the
patrol wagon and placed alongside the de-
vices taken from the Beede games. The
dealers of the two houses were
then put in the wagon and the
officers, who guarded the entrances to the
rooms, withdrew. Instantly the players
swarmed out like bees from hive they
were not sure but that the officers had
made mistake and still intended to ar
rest them, and they were consequently
very anxious to make their escape while
there ~ as an opportunity.


The names of the eleven dealers who
were arrested are l.. Bow and Charles
Isaacs, from the Delcho; J. E. Griffin, G..
II. Sleitzer, G. Spaulding and C. Moore,
from the Horseshoe; Pop" Dolan, James
Burns and G. W. Griffin from the NJ. & n. I;

SPOKANE, March 1S.--Details of what
appears to be one of the most mysteri-
GUS and villainous murders ever COM
mitted in this section came to light at
Rockford, town forty miles from this
city, today. William Thurman, A. L.
Richardson and Mrs. Thurman are
missing, and the indications are that
Thurman was murdered by his wife and
her paramour, who then took
flight. Richardson is a worthless
drunken fellow whose children have
been charge upon the county, but he
succeeded in gaining the affections of
Mrs. Thurman, who had always been
considered model wife. Thurman pro-
tested and elected Richardson from his
house, but the woman took his part and
allowed him to visit her when
ever Thurman was absent. There
appears to have been good deal of
strife between the husband and wife and
his life was threatened, for he recently
took counsel with his friends relative to
OuO 6CCPo HO OuSHt w tdke 10 protect

avoiding the publicity of the courts. As
Thurman had not been seen for some
time, Monday two of his brothers went
to his place. They found it deserted,

evidently having escaped through small

A realistic story
Without any gush or glory
Yet this fellow Ebenezer

Governor Brown, of Maryland, has
been forced by public opinion in that
state to command Mrs. Brown to put
aside queenly crown. The story is
that Mrs Brown, having some hand
some diamonds, had mind to have
them reset for the Inauguration cere-
monies and reception. She carried them
to Baltimore jeweler, who suggested
that they should be arranged in crown
or tiara. After some hesitation Mrs.
Brown accepted the design for crown.
In due time the crown was completed,
and was written up by the Baltimore
papers. Then the trouble began for the
governor. Some papers announced that
Mrs. Brown would wear crown on all
public occasions, just like a real queen.
Others varied the announcement by say
ing that Mrs. Brown considered the
crown as the outward and visible symbol
lady of the state.


Immediately the people of Maryland
caught fire, and asked on what meat
had their Caesar fed that his family
should put on a style not authorized by
the constitution. There must have been
a terrible struggle in the governors
mind, for governors are but human after
all. Eventually the statesman triumphed
over the husband, and Mrs. Brown did
not wear crown. Neither was there
any special ceremonies attendant upon
the Inauguration, which were made
severely simple, even Jeffersonian in
their simplicity. Transcript

entirely consumed.

ing were ordered to put escapes on
their building, and Seton reported that
the order was obeyed. 1t now trans
pires that his report was false, and that

MYRTLE CREEK STATION, April 29-TSpe-
cial. The north bound California express
was wrecked q mile north Of here this
morning. 1t was the work of train-wreck-
ers. Two ties were placed crosswise on the
track. and the engine, mail and express
cars were ditched. Engineer Morris
jumped and was cut and bruised about the
head. but otherwise uniniured. Fireman
George Golling was caught between the
tender and the tank, his legs were broken
IN two places and he was severely scalded.
OF five tramps between the express and
mail cars, one was caught and badly in
jured. The accident was fortunate from
the fact that no one was killed. The en-
glne lies on the right side of the right
track, the tender jammed into the
cab. The mail car partly lies on the
engine with one side entirely torn
away. The postal clerk escaped unhurt
by miracle. He was in the back end of
the car, tying up tine Roseburg mail. Ex-
press Messenger Applegate was standing
before his desk. When the crash came he
seized the rods overhead and swung him.
self off the floor. The freight was all
thrown into the front of the car, and the
messenger says be would have been killed
had he stayed on thu aoor. The train fell
toward the bank. There is steep bank
sloping to the river. If the train had gone
over the bank the loss of life would have
been fearful. Wrecking trains are at hand
ard the wreck is being cleared away. The
track was torn up badly for 200 feet.
There is no clue to the perpetrators.
Robbery is supposed to have been the
object.

Three men are alive at Niagara Falls who can
recite thrilling story of adventure that few
would care to experience These three men,
Edward Kearney, 7. j. Riley and X. Nately,
were rescued from a boat in the midst Of the
rapids just above the cataract.


They were the crew of barge in tow Of .
small tug which had started out the other day
from Port Day. which is the inlet to the old
hydraulic canal. and considered the nearest
point that boat can safely approach the
rapids above the falls The boat was laden
with fifty tons of cut stone.


just as the tug with its tow reached the
stream cled1 of the shore the tow line suddenly
snapped. The barge with its human freight
instantly shot down the rapids toward tine falls.
Her speed was increasing every minute and the
fate of her crew seemed certain.


Suddenly the craft stopped as il by the
rest of a Proyidential hand. She had struck a
rock or rather had run into a fork between two
rocks, and was stuck fast. The waters seethed
and boiled and bubbled by. but the men were
safe for the time being.


Now came the rescue, in which Fred. Robin
son, VIM. Fleck and Frank White figured as the
heroes. These young fellows, all stalwart and
brave. secured small row boat and long coil
of rope. One end of the rope was made fast
10 snOre. anu TWO OF tne reSCuer5 manned the

sage being guided to shore by the boatmen
ctnging 90 the rope.


Altogether six perilous trips. three out and

The Mayor Signs the Pledge.


MONTREAL, April 1S-Fathers Doyle, Smith,
Otis and Hecklinger Of the Paulist Fathers OF
New York concluded the monster mission al
ST. Patrick's Church last night. The mission
has been one OF the most striking
ever held in Montreal. During its
progress over 5000 people signed the total
abstinence pledge and ffty-six converts were
received into the church.


The fathers strongly Denounced the Mon
treal civic authorities for their apathy in not
enforcing the liquor laws. The instrumentation
was made i'll the presence OF Mayor McShane
and a number of other prominent city officials
and produced great sensation. The
effect was SO great that Mayor McShane and
other officials were led to sign the pledge. A
large sum of money was collected during the
mission to assist in educating young Catholic
missionaries at the Catholic University in
Washington.


Fathers Doyle and Smith leave at once for
Connecticut to commence mission there.

the Suez canal and the Dardanelles. The
sending Of relief ships from the eastern
and western coasts, would, the commit
tee thinks, be spectacle for the ad-
miration OF the civilized world, weaving
thus in unison the bright ribbon of
Christian charity around the whole
earth. In order that the Pacific move
ment may be in the highest degree sue
cessful, the committee invokes the aid
of the state authorities, municipalities,
industrial and charitable organizations,
the clergy and press OF the entire Pacific
slope.

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 29. .--Solly Smith.
Of Los Angeles, and George Siddons, of

the California Athletic club tonight.
The men weighed about 1l91a pounds
each. Smith was the favorite in the
betting.


Smith scored two right-handers on the

In the second round, he chased the
New Yorker about the ring, giving him
both hands about the head and smash
ing him in the face with bis left when
he could get inside OF Siddons' guard,
which the latter kept about his face.
The New Yorker made no effort to re-
taliate but stood the punishment man.
fully.


Smith landed three hard left-handers

the next three rounds. But Smiths
rushes were fruitless, as the New Yorker
kept his guard up we'll.


Siddons scored couple of lefts on

confident.


The sixth round was marked by more

apparently seeking to tire Smith.


From the seventh to the thirteenth,

In the twenty-sixth, Siddons nearly

The fight was not very fast after that.
Siddons continued to take most of the
blows, which were aimed for his head,
on his gloves, occasionally parrying or
stopping with an upper-cut. Smith
was doing mcst of the work, but his
blows were gradually lacking steam.


Forty rounds had been fought at
midnight and neither man had any ad-
vantage.


Little was done from the fortieth to
the end of the fiftieth round. At the
end of the fifty-fiith round, not blow
having been struck since the fiftieth,
Referee Cook consulted the principals
and nnnnuncnd- that -thay- -had -g~eraaA
rnar they could not finish the contest
tonight, and that he would reserve his
decision until the meeting OF the board
of directors next Monday evening.


Siddons evidently sought at the out
set to make a draw, and Smiths
strength failed him after Is rounds of
good work on his part.

MADRID, Dec. 1.--This has been day OF
tumult and apprehension throughout the
city. Thousands Of men did not go to
work at the usual hour, but waited
in groups on street corners near
the center of the city. They
were joined by crowds of loafers.
anarchists and rowaies. Thousands gath
cred in the Puer.a del Sol and began
shouting against she ministry and the
municipal authorities. The police tried
to dispense them, bat were repulsed. Re-
Inducements were called, but before they
arrived most of the crowd had drifted into
side streets.


At 2 O'Clock the crowd gathered again,
II 900 or H. 600 strong. Black hags were
numerous, and many men were arrested
with clubs. The crowd surged, up to
the steps of the nome office shouting:
"Down with the government" "Down
with the city thieves" Crush the upper
ten thousand" "GiSe US our rights" etc.
The building was closed and call sent
out for more military and police protec-
ton. Before the troops arrived the cry,
''To the palace" was raised, and the
mob started down the Gale, del Arsenal
shouting, singing and waving flags.
Stones, clubs and pieces of metal from the
workshops were thrown through the win
dows on both sides ef the street. Respect
able citizens were thrown down and
trampled on or compelled to join the mob.
and several shops were forced and plum
dered.


When half way to the palace. the rear
end of the mob was intercepted and dis
persed by the police. who broke in from
side street with drawn sabers. The strug-
gle lasted ten minutes, as the men fought
back stubbornly with whatever weapons
they could find. The policemen were
knocked senseless with stones, and
two market women who joined the
mob were cut down with sabers. Mean
while, the foremost of the mob
reached the open square before the palace.
They shouted for Justice to the poor"
the dismissal of tie ministry and the
punishment of the principal officials
who were stealing the peoples money. A
body of mounted police charged upon them
down the Gale del Arsenal, and after an
other struggle dispersed them. Several
persons were injured in the tight. The
leaders of the rioters were captured.


After the fight the rioters gathered in
groups on the street corners, there being
thousand or more, and sang the Puerta
del Sol.


During this demonstration Senior Sa-
gasta, ex-prime minister, passed by and
was greeted with cheers from all sides.


Tonight the guaros at the government
buildings and palace were doubled. The
uneas:ness felt by the Weather classes is

A collision occurred between the steamers

escaping being sunk and her wheel and fantails
being completely demolished. The accident
was due to the dense fog.

rounded Alki point the Perley hove in sight,

sighted uatil they had come within 100 yards Of

nard to port, and the boat answered 80 quickly

oil the Flyer also threw his helm to port, but

swer readily enough to pass, but struck

struck . few feet further forward nothing
could have saved her from sinking and several

drowned.

Glide brought her passengers and freight into

the only blame that attaches to anybody for the

Furnishing Them.


PARIS, Nov. 11.-Many accusations
have been made that German agents in
Dahomey furnished King Behanzin with
quick firing rifles. These have been de-
MED by the Germans, who asserted that
if Behanzin had such weapons, he pro-
cured them from the British. The lat
ter assertions are borne out by a capture
just made off the coast of Dahcmey.
The Brandon, French dispatch boat,
cruising off the Dahomeyan coast, sur
prised the British steamer John Holly,
with cargo of Winchester rifles and
ammunition, beyond all doubt intended
for the Dahomeyan army. The vessel
was seized and the cargo confiscated.
The matter will undoubtedly be made
the subject of diplomatic remonstrance.
