Dead Miners Rescued From Their Un-


timely Tomb.


DUNBAR, Pa, March 24.-The dead
have been rescued from their untimely
tomb, and all that remains now is to
afford Christian burial to the miners
who met their fate in the Hill Farm
mine, June 10, 1890. The twenty-three
bodies found yesterday will be brought
to the surface for burial today. Six
more unfortunates cannot be recovered
until the water is all pumped out.
When found the bodies were huddled
together, showing that the imprisoned
miners had fed as far from death as
possible. The bodies were contorted in
ghastly shapes, indicating that the
miners had suffered the most horrible
tortures before death. The owners OF
the mine have expended 100000 in ac-
complshing the rescue of the bodies.

First Engineer Homand, aged about so,

last man lost.


Second Engineer James Burns, aged

board before the vessel struck. The rest
of the crew were saved.

for San Francisco tomorrow. The captain

text:
How the Poisoner of Unfortunate Girls


Met His Doom.


LONDON, Nov. 15.-Thomas Neill, alias
Cream, the murderer of Matilda Cloves
and several other unfortunat girls, paid
the penalty for his crimes at 9 o'clock
this morning. Notwithstanding the or
der that the execution should be pri-
vate, representative OF the Associated
Press was admitted to the prison. Neill
spent restless night and this morning
paid little heed to the mlnistratlons OF
the chaplain.


Hangman Ellington entered the cell
few minutes before 8, and with his as-
sistants, fastened leather belt around
the condemned mans waist. Straps
from this securely pinioned his arms at
the elbows and wrists. Neill submitted
quietly, without utteripg a word. The
procession to the gallows was then
formed, headed by the chief deputy,
followed by the chaplain reading the
burial service. Neill came next with a
warder on either side. He walked
firmly, though deadly pallor over
spread his face which, however, showed
no other signs of emotion. The hang
man brought up the rear.


Arrived at the scaffold, white cap
was pulled down over his eyes, and Bill
lington guided him on the trap door
beneath the cross from which the rope
dangled. The hangman' g assistants then
deity pinioned Nelll's legs. The moose
was adjusted around his neck, the exc
cutioner stepped back, pressed lever,
and Neill fell five feet into the pit.
There were convulslve twitchings of the
murderer for a few seconds, then the
body hung motionlees. Death was evil
IDENTIFY instantaneous and painless.


Neill was remarkably calm and self
possessed throughout. Just before the
cap was drawn down he thanked the
prison officials for their kindness. He
seemed resigned to his fate. He told the
undersherif that the last two days had
been the calmest and happiest of his life.
He declined to take stimulants to sus-
tain him for the final ordeal. Ellington
says he acted remarkably cool, and al
most placed himself on the trap with
out directions.


The body was cut down after banging
an hour, and a cast of the head was
taken. The coroner's jury viewed the
body and returned verdict in accord
ance with the facts. The remains were
placed in a coffin with quicklime and
buried under the fagstones of the prison
corridor, where have been buried the
remains of a long line of noted GRIM
inals.

The Rodrigue brothers. who stole the we'll

then murdered nine men to cover up their
villainy. have been executed at Manila. The
news comes by way of Singapore and forms the
closing chapter of one of the worst stories of
South Sea crime.


The Rodrigues were sent to the penal colony
at New Caledonia, but about three years ago
escaped to Cape Colony. They made some
money in the diamond fields and then drifted
to Tahiti. There they picked up many South
Sea dialects and traded among the islands.
They found the old king yacht was to be sent
out on trading expedition, with a good outfit
and $4,000 in coin. The night before she was
to sail they stole her, and. with a crew they had
bribed with offers of large wages sailed for the
Caroline Islands. The brothers corrupted the
native cook, Moloi. and induced him to poison
the seven native sailors. When these men were
helpless they shot down the white captain and
the sapercargo. After this they watched their
victims die in terrible agony and amused them
selves by tossing their bodies to the sharks.


The three men then cruised around the
Islands and made their way to Manila. There
the cook demanded his part of the plumber. but
the brothers refused and threatened him with

James Clark Carman was arraigned today
on a charge of having caused the death of
her stepdaughter, aged years. She was
committed for trial, and her husband Sc
verely cenSlred for not having prevented

was treated with the greatest brutal
ity, being often tied to banisters

stretch. Mrs. Clark frequently beat her
terribly with strap or heavy cane, and
often, when she claimed the girl was tell
ing falsehoods, she tied a string tightly
about her tongue and left her for hours to
suffer excrutiating torture. The child
finally gave way and died. A physician
testified that but for the ill-usage to which
she ives subjected and lack of food the
child would have been perfectly healthy.

| By the Associated Press.


| SAN Francisco, Nov. 30.-The storm


which ragged here last night and this


morning was the worst for many years
| and did great damage. The wind at


tanned velocity of 72 miles an hour,


and was accompanied by furious rain
which flooded the streets and broke the


sewers. At the Potrero, where the
Union Iron works and other manufaetur-


ing interests are located, the wind played


havoc. A number of houses occupied

mates were compelled to seek refuge in
stronger structures. A Chinese lodging

toppled over and one of them
killed. Several others were bad
ly bruised. A cottage on Bernal

already deserted it. The roof over the
stage of the Tivoli was blown off and the
scenery spoiled. A story frame

street ball grounds, was completely
wrecked, as was cottage in Vallejo.
In Golden Gate park several hundred
trees were blown down, the shrubbery
was injured and the roof of the Casino
blown away.


On the water front and on the bay the
extreme force of the wfhd was felt.
Ferryboats were unable to make regular
trips, owing to the roughnees of the
water, and passengers who came across
were badly frightened. Ships were bat
tered and driven about in a terrible
manner. The big ship Palgrave, lying

schooner Caroline Dickson, loaded with

wharf and is wreck. The schooner

big fishing smack Stella was driven

tling with the gale for So hours.


The gale began to come up early in

blowing " miles an hour at Point Lobos.

house veranda and the spray was car
ried clean over the building and into the
road beyond. Telegraph wires were all

Grated to 60 miles an hour, and at 8

report came from Berkeley that num-
Der of fishing boats had been capsized,

damage was done to boat houses. The
yacht Fearless was wrecked, and the

"Sheep," said Engineer Willard
"cause more trouble than any other
stock. An engineer always tries to
guard against killing stock, but if l had
my choice would rather run into cat
tie, horses, hogs cr any other animals,
rather than sheep. Many thousands of
sheep are in the great focks that some
times cross the tracks of western rail
roads. Where there are no fences quick
turn in the road through cut may find
the locomotive moving right through
them. 1t is well known how sheep fol-
low their leader Notwithstanding the
moving train they continue to rush un-
der the cars, and sometimes many are
killed that the locomotive never touched.
They really commit suicide, crowding
under the wheels before the train can be
stopped.


Sometimes over 200 or 300 sheep have
been killed. But the wool gets into the
running gear of the engine, and this
causes the engineer more trouble than
the killing of other stock. Sometimes
the engineer is compelled to stop and
clean out the wool that works its way
into the more delicate machinery. At
the end of the trip a search is also made
for wool that may have escaped the at
tention of the engineer in his examina-

the plaza were quickly surrounded and the
barbecue commenced. Hundreds of men,

International Copyright Law.


LONDON, Feb. l5.-Seven months have passed
since the United States copyright bill became
law. From the very first it has been the
cynosure OF British authors and publishers.
and still more OF British printers
and inquiries made in all directions
prove that they are closely conyersant with ths
measure. There is no indifference, no ignor-
ance on the subject, but Intelligent and inter-
ested familiarity. With a few exceptions the
responsible Representatives of the firms ap-
preached in this inquiry discussed the question
without Reserve, and there was no hiding be-
hind business arrangements any other
transparent excuse. Some gentlemen frankly
admitted that their dealings with American
publishers since the act passed had been
limited, and that they could not well
claim TO base the expression of their
views on actual experience, but q careful and
constant study has enabled them TO form judg-
ments and well defined anticipations. The
opinions collected may be briefly summarized
thus: Authors like the law; publishers don't
mind it; some regard II with favor; printers
and book manufacturers hate it.

Never forget that publishing is busi-

connected with philanthropy, charity or
pure love Of literature. You have to
do with business men.

Another literary monument Is gone.
Those who knew Grub street-now Milton
street-wll remember quaint little square
which stood on its western side. 1t was
poor kind OF square, writes Mr.. Besant,
standing round paved court; vehicles
except the coster's barrow-could not enter
there. The houses were small and mean,
yet they had the eighteenth-century air.
The rest Of the street was built up with
vast warehouses. This alone remained of
the glorious past. Into this corner had been
driven the real associations Of Grub street.
Oae knew every room In every house. In
this starved Boyes; in this, Otway. Here
two translators occupied one room and
shared one bed, one blanket and one shirt.


johnson knew this square. Goldsmith
oft en- came here when he had any money to
give 1t away among his poorer brothers.
Very few Of them went about the streets in
complete absence of anxiety concerning the
Sheriff's man and the Compter Sunday
was day Of relief. Hero Smollett made
the acquaintance of my Lord Potatoe. The
square was fragrant with the memories OF
the starveiing bards. Sham travellers
abounded here who had never been beyond
Greenwich. Greek scholars who knew
not the alphabet, essayists on polite society
who never advanced beyond sixpenny
ordinary. But now the square is gone and a
great warehouse stands upon the spot.
Grub street Is, indeed, no more.

river was within one inch last Saturday
night of the highest point ever reached
at the same date, having risen fourteen
inches during the week. The river has
cut out an immense channel at the
crevasse made last year at fifteen miles
below Ell Rio, and at least three-fourths
of the water in the Colorado is running
to the southwest into lake Jullulu and
New river. Carter river and Riley
slough, which supply water that runs
into Salton through East river, and
which were damned at the mouth by
drift few days ago, are being opened
again by the rice in the Colorado.

During this time of year the hands and
face should be carefully cared for. Peo-
pie of light complexion usually suffer
greatly during cold weather from chap
ped hands and faces. There are many
preparations for sale at the drug stores
for chapped hands and all are good
enough, but very simple way to keep

sore is to rub them with the juice OF a
lemon. Then wash them well, rub in a
little vaseline or glycerin, and powder
them well with starch.


The lemon juice removes all little par

whitens the skin. The occasional use of
lemon juice on both the face and hands
will keep them white and soft, and pre-
vent the necessity of washing them sew
eral times day with soap. Use soap
sparingly on hands, neck and face dur
ing cold weather, and use only the best,
with tepid water.--Interview in st.

CADIZ, Oct. 10.- Enormous crowds
watched the departure of the gunboat
Conde Vallerno, conveying Queen Regent
Christina and the royal party to
Huelva, where they will take part in
the Columbus celebration. The gum
boat was escorted by fleet of foreign
warships. When the warship arrived
Oft Huelva she was met by Senior Cano-
vas Delcastilo, the municipal authori-
ties, diplomats who are visiting Huelva,
and other dignitaries. Twenty-three
Spanish and foreign men-of-war were
ranged in line, and, as the gunboat
With the royal party on board entered
the bay, the nearest war ship fred
royal salute. This was repeated by the
next ship in line, and so on until every
one of the 20 vessels had saluted little
King Alfonso. who, with his mother, on
the Copde Vallerno, came to anchor off
the Monastery La Rabida. The royal
party was taken ashore, and to the old
monastery where Columbus received his
fret encouragement in the scheme which
led to the discovery of the new world.
After inspecting the venerable pile, the
royal party returned to the gunboat,
which then proceeded to Huelva. The
queen regent and King Alfonso will dis
embark in state tomorrow.

BUTTE, April 12.-[Special.l- disas-

smelter of the Butte and Boston Company.
The loss is estimated at $3.50. 600; insur-
ance, 10000. The fire caught by the in
tense heat from the furnace which was be-

well equipped with hose, but by the falling
in of the brick wall at one end of the
mammoth structure, the water main was
bursted. The heat was intense and drove
the men back fifty feet. Efforts were now
directed to saving the silver mill and con-
centrator on either side, which were sue
cessful.

two huge furnaces with capacity of 500
tons of ore per day. Within fifteen min
utes after the start of the fire the stacks
were standing alone, each over 100 feet
high, amid the settings of the fire. This
was one of the largest copper smelling
plants in the state. Eight O'Hara fur
paces, six Buckners and four reverbera-
tory blast furnaces were totally destroyed.
Five hundred men were thrown out of
employment.

Two shapes were walking on the strand
One starlit night in no mans land;
Two shapes that during earthly life
Gave hate for hate in deadly strife.
They met. Swift forth their falchions flew;
Each pinned the other through and through;
Yet neither fell. Again they strove
For mastery, and madly drove
To right and left their falchions bright,
Nor sound nor cry profaned the night.
Through corselet, casque and visor, too,
AS through the air their swift blades flew;
Until amazed, they stood aghast,
And on the sands their weapons cast.
Then laughed they both at mortal strife.
The passing dream of earthly life.
And clasping each the others hand
They walk the shades of no mans land.

Brass andirons, big and little, may be
bought in the antique shops at from
$3.50 to $40 pair. The most highly
priced irons are called Chippendales.
The characteristic Of the Chippendale is
q shaft in three parts, that nearest the
feet being hexagonal, the next large and
egg shaped and the top repeating the
same egg form in about one-third the
diameter.


Another favorite form is characterized
by small vase, like Colonial sugar
bowl, at the top; long, slender shaft,
with Corinthian capital, on which the
vase rests, and base that often has
three feet. Some of these have the rear
horizontal bar crooked, so that short
leg may be held without bringing the
vertical shafts too close together. Just
at the bend usually rises second and
smaller shaft of brass.-New York Sun.

Another coal-laden ship las been burned


at sea- and the probabilities are that half


her crew has met watery grave. The fine


German ship Clara, bound from Liverpool
to this port, must now be added to the list


of vessels already reported as destroyed
during the last few months by spontaneous
combustion. The news was brought to


san Francisco by the British ship Califor-
MIA that arrived in port last evening, having


on board Captain Kuhlmann and twelve Of


the crew of the ill-fated ship.


The Clara sailed from Liverpool for this


port pa days ago and bad luck seems to


have attended her from the start. Soon
after clearing the channel she was caught
in q gale that lasted five days, and besides


suffering other slight damages her rudder-
head was twisted. Although i was patched


as we'll as possible under the circumstances
and answered we'll enough iii fine weather


it broke off short in the first blow that the
ship was IN.


Recourse was then had to the monkey


filler and the ship was headed for Rio de


Janeir0, where she arrived on October 10.


Here the ruddPr was repaired and once


more Captain Kuhlmann set out on his


long voyage 10 San Francisco, which port,


however, his ship was destined never 10


reach.


HOVE TO OFF CAPE HORN.
Off Cape Horn the weather was unusually
severe and the ship was compelled to neaYo
TO for several days, and also suffered the
loss OF many OF her sails. Nothing very
serious occurred, however, until the ship
was in latitude 20 south and about los


west, when fire was discovered in the cargo.


The pumps were rugged and torrents of
water flowed into the hold. For time 1t
seemed as if the fire had been qutnched,
but such was not the case, however, and
the crew of the vessel found that instead OF
being put out the fire still Smodered and
the ship was a floating volcano. Once more
the pumps were put to work and holes cut
in the deck through which the streams OF
water was turned on the burning mass be-
low


Finding that this would not subdue the
flames the matches were taken of and the
work of digging down to the fire began. In
spite Of the intense heat the men worked
like beavers, and they had good reason to


work for their ship was over 1000 miles
from land and no help In sight
For forty-eight hours they shOveled and
dug until the heat became too great TO bear,
and the glowing mass OF coal sent out dense
volumes of binding smoke that threatened


to suffocate them. Again the matches were
battened down and tons Of water pumped


into the ship, but the fire rapidly glined,
and soon the pitch in the decks began to


boil.


DRINKING WATER HEATED.


Even the water in the tanks became hot


enough to send a cloud Of steam up through


the fresh-water pump. Then Captain kuhl-


mann realized the dread truth ;hat the ship
was doomed TO destruction and reluctantly
gave the order to clear away the boats.
The crew numbered twenty-Six all told,
and when the only two boats available we're


lowered the captain and twelve men entered
one and the mate with the others manned
the remaining boat.


BY wise provision in the German marine
laws each ship boat is provided with box
containing charts, compass, seXtant and
nautical almanac, while breakers Of water
and bread and beef are also slowed in the
boats Thus the crew had food enough 10
last at least fourteen days and longer if put
on short allowance.


Both boats were furnished with a chrO-
nometer and mate and captain had the
necessary instruments 10 find the latitude
and longitude. The boats left the burning
ship about shutdown in latitude south,
longitude ll2 west, but remained close TO
her during the night The castaways did
not leave her any too soon, for about 10
o'clock the flames burst from the hatch
ways and in a short time the fine vessel was
on fire from stem TO stern.


A GRAND SPECTACLE PRESENTED.
Mast after mast and sail after sail were
soon in flames and afforded a grand and
solemn spectacle, as, waited by ligh I
breeze, she slowly sailed along on fire from
truck TO keel.


! daylight nothing was left but burned


and charred hulk that took a final
plunge aud disappeared beneath the waves.
The two boats then shaped their course
toward the MarquesaS Islands, distant at
| least 1000 miles but the sea was smooth
and the trade winds steadily waited them
toward the haven OF refuge.
The boats kept close together until night
came, and then were separated in the dark
ness. For six days the boat In which Cap
tain kuhlmaun was sailed steadily on her
course, and during that time only one blow
occurred. and that only lasted twelve hours,
and the men had no difficulty in riding il
out, assisted by a sea lanchOr formed of the
oars and sail.


On the afternoon of the sixth day sail


was sighted and to the JOY OF the ship
wrecked men she was seen to be bearing
down toward them. She proved TO be the
| British ship California, bound from New
castle, y. ). w, 10 San Francisco.
RECEIVED WITH OPEN ARMS.
Captain Dickinson received the ship
wrecked men with open arms and made
them as comfortable as possible, while the
opened their chests and shared their cloth


NJ with the unfortunate sailors There
S a possibility that the mates boat


may have been picked up by passing yes
sci, or she may have reached the islands;


but this is considered doubtful. as the day


after the captains boat was picked up a


strong gale commenced. that lasted several


days. and the boat and all she contained


may have gone to the bottom in the heavy
sea.


The Clara was owned by d. II Watjen &
Co. of Bremen, and was built ut Bremen


haven in 1882 She was wooden vessel of


1857 tous register, and has been in San


Francisco several times. The cargo MAS


consigned to Meyer Wilson & Co.. and


was fully insured. There was no insurance


on the ship and the loss will fall altogether


on the owners.


BY a strange fatality the Clara and the i'll


fated American ship Rappahannock lay


side by side in the docks a. Liverpool, and


both loaded coal for this port at the same


time and both were des lroyed at sea in the


same manner except that the American ship


was carried into Juan Fernandez before


she was consumed, and thus the crew
escaped the long and dangerous voyage in
open boats, which fell TO the lot OF the


Clara's crew.

The tow boat Webster and two scows belong
ing to the department of street cleaning of New
York drifted out to sea yesterday morning and
for long time grave apprehension was felt for
the safety of the crew of the Webster and of the
sixty odd Italians employed upon the scow
This apprehension was partially allayed in the
afternoon upon the receipt of dispatch to the
effect that the Webster and the scows had been
rescued off Fire Island.


The tugs Webster and Nichols, each towing
two scows loaded with refuse. started ont to sea
to the dumping grounds early yesterday morn
ing. A heavy sea was running and the wind
was blowing furiously, which caused the little
steamers to labor considerably in the heavy
seaway. When oil Rockawav Beach the tow
ing hawser of the Webster fouled her screw,
disabling the vessel, and she was rapidly
driven out to sea by the high wind. The
Nichols, seeing the predicament of her COM
panion vessel, anchored her tow, upon which
there were about seyenty-tive Italian laborers
In Gravesend bay, and started to assist the
Webster.


Her efforts to tow the drifting vessels. were
however, futile. and she finally abandoned them
and her own tow and ran up to the city tor
aid.


The Nichols captain reported that the Ital-
lans on the scows were terror stricken, and
they had just cause to be. They were on open
scows in "A high sea amid a terrific gale and
the day was bitterly cold. too. 1t was prob
able That at any momeTA they might be blown
washed off the scOws and drowned. The
captain said that it was impossible for him to
approach the scows which had been anchored
without endangering his own boat and tho
scows because the waves and wind were SO
high.


Several tugs were at once sent out by the
street-cleauing department to search for the
Webster, while two others were dispatched to
Gravesend bay. Late in the afternoon dis
patches were received stating that the Webster
and her tow had been rescued off Fire Island
Nothing, however, had been heard from the
scows anchored in Gravesend bay.

ticulars, and signed the documents. A
cablegram was sent to Johnston, and his
reply should be received tomorrow.

A most remarkable phenomenon was wit
messed at Traxase City. Mich. At a few
minutes before o'clock the wells at the
water-wOrks and electric light plants gave
out simultaneously. The men at the plants
began investigating, compared notes, and
concluded that the intake pipes from the
bay had been blocked by floating ice.


They went to the bay to investigate and
found the bottom of the bay entirely bare
for fully a hundred feet from the usual
shore line. The water had fallen fully
seven feet. BOATS OF all kinds, steam and
sail, were grounded. Docks were high and
dry upon the beach. and pleasure cottages
that but an hour before had their steps
Tapped by the waters Of the bay were now
seven or eight rods from the water line


For fully an hour the city was in total
darkness and many assembled al the beach
and upon the docks to view the curious
phenomenon.


Then with a mighty rush the waters came
back to their natural place with the force
Of tidal wave. The waves tumbled over each
other as though laSned by mighty wind,
and their tops threw clouds OF ray many
feet into the air. Boats were washed from
their mOoTings and cast many feet upon the
beach; dock piles were lOOsened ana came
tumbllng into shore with the rushing
waters, and the doors and windows Of many
Of the cottages were smashed in.


Tie damage was considerable, especially
to shipping. Once before this fall the
water ID the bay fell five and half feet ia
two days. but this sudden fall discount
any record kept by the oldest Inhabitants.
As 10 strong breeze was blowing from off
shore the mystery seems the more mex
plcabe Some express the belief that the
curious phenomenon was due to seismic in
fuences, yet in this latitude such disturb
ances are scarcely known, and other shore
cities would certainly have noted like fail
Of the water if this had been the cause.

PINoLE, CAL, March 2S.-An explosion
occurred at the California Powder
works this morning, entirely destroying
the nitroglycerine mixing house. All
the buildings OF the works were more or
less damaged. The cause was the over
heating of one OF the air-heaters.


Four thousand, five hundred pounds
of nitroglycerine were destroyed. Four
men were at work in the building, and
when the foreman saw there was no
possibility of preventing the accident he
gave the alarm to his fellow-workmen
and they made good their escape.


The shock was telt for miles around
and soon messengers came pouring in
from all directions, making inquiry
either for friends of relatives, who were
at work for the powder company. The
total loss of property will reach twenty
thousand dollars.


The Oregon express was just rounding
the curve when the explosion took place,
and the passengers jumped to their feet
and thought dynamiters were at work.


Pieces of the destroyed building were
picked up two miles distant.

BY the Associated Press.


SAN Francisco, May 25.-The crew Of
the ship st. Charles, which was blown
up off the Oregon coast on the 18th in
slant, arrived here today on the steamer
Willamette Valley. The st. Charles left
Nanaino with cargo OF coal May 18th
and experienced heavy seas for three
days. On the morning of the 18th the
second mate, Mike Flynn, and Charles
Lenberg, sailor. went to the fore hatch
to get some potatoes, taking with them
the ships lantern. Louis Strandburg, a
sailor, spoke to the men and saw the
mate pass Lenberg the lantern. Lenberg
was reaching through hole into the
fore part of the ship, and was about to
crawl through, when an explosion oc-
cured and Flynn was lifted bodily in
the air. He fell at Strandberg's feet
with great hole in his scalp and his
legs burned to crisp. Lenberg was
thrown back against ladder and was
terribly cut and burned. f


Strandburg's beard was einged by the
flames, which shot from the hole, follow
ing the roar Of the explosion. Ned Kiley,
sailor, who was on deck at the time,
states that when the explosion occurred,
the ropes, hawsers and main hatch were
hurled from the deck by the force, and
the deck opened wide from the after
part of the house to the stern. The
spanker-boom was carried away, the
wheel-house tipped over. and the ship
generally demolished. The rigging was
on fire and the pumps would not work.


Captain Chapman was found pinned
to the floor in his cabin under an over
turned sofa and book case. The cap
tain's spine was broken, and he was in
great agony. The men extricated him
with difficulty from among the shattered
timbers. and made haste to get into the
boats, as the vessel was sinking. There
were nineteen men divided among the
three small boats.


When last seen the st. Charles's main
sail was afire and the ship laundering.
The boats were 200 miles from land,
without a compass. They succeeded in
making Cape Foulweather safely, and
there Captain Chapman died. Lenberg
and Second Mate Flynn were taken to
Newport, Ore, by the survivors, who
then came to this city. Flynn is ex-
pected to die. The sailors believe coal
gas, ignited by the lantern, caused the
explosion. ,f aeq

Orang-outangs, lions, tigers, hippo
potami, elephants and the other repre-
seutatives Of the animal kingdom from
every country in the world spent quiet
Sunday with their attendants on the
circus lot in west indianapolis.


The managers go to Sunday school,
the performers recuperate, the canvas
men and drivers sleep, and in fact every-
body rests except the attendants in the
menagerie. The eorang-outang must have
his whiskers trimmed, the lion his toes
manicured, and Che elephant must have
. sponge bath and his corns pared.
The hippopotainus perspires blood dur
ing the whole week, and unless his
rough skin is washed on Sunday a black
crust forms and he gets sscaly." The
American water is not 81 soft and free
from alkali as his native water of CEN
trail Africa and his teeth get coated with
matter resembling the sediment of a tea
kettle. On Sunday his mouth must be
pried open and his teeth cleaned and
brushed with scented tooth powder made
from the pulverized bark of tree which
grows on the banks of the Lukuga river
In Africa. If his teeth were not thus
preserved they would decay in three
years and dyspepsia would send him to
q premature grave in foreign land.


The toe nails Of the lion grow long and
sharp. Twice year they must be
trimmed with clippers to keep them
from tearing each other to pieces in
their family brawls. The tigers and the
bears rub against their cages SO much
that sore spots break out and they must
be healed with iniment and medicated
oils. In fact all animals must receive
treatment Of some kind. As their regu-
lar keepers alone understand how to
treat them, Sunday is thus busy day.


When the representatives Of the city
papers visited the menagerie they found
the lions roaring and much excited.
Near one of the cages two men held
down on the ground q cub, while Lion
Tanner Conkling with large pair OF
nippers was clipping its toe nails. There
were four cubs in the cage, and one by
one they were taken out Of the cage by
Conkling and their nails cut short.
While this operation was going on the
ioness was crying piteously and she'd
ding great tears. No human mother
could show more parental solicitude for
its offspring than this queen of animals.
The lions in another cage 100 feet dis
tant almost chilled ones blood with
their terrible roars while the cubs were
undergoing the operation.


The elephants seemed to be having the
best of the day. They were being sponged
with soft warm water and enjoyed the
bath hugely. An old elephant had
corn on one of his fore feet and he grace
fully rested it in stall while his at
tendant removed it with razor. After
the lion cubs had been attended to
Tanner Conkling entered the cage Of
three huge lions which Mr.. Perley said
was the biggest cage of lions in America.
Two are Asiatic aad one is African.
The latter, the largest and most noble
of the lot, had sore paw, which Conk-
ling took In his lap and rubbed with
black, waxy substance, which he said
was distilled from the sap Of an African
tree growing near Timbuctoo. Near by
was cage of hyenas in which the keeper
was washing the sore eye of AN old one
who, the keeper explained, had chewed
of the lip Of his predecessor.


A double horned rhincceros, which
has worn out his horns rubbing them
against the bars, submitted to thor
ough scrubbing from the hands of man

BY the Associated Press


LONDON, May. 20.-Baron de Worms.
parliamentary secretary for the colonial
office, read telegram in the house of
commons this afternoon confirming the
terrible disaster caused by the hurricane
in the island OF Mauritius, April Goth.
1t said one-third of the capital city,
Port Louis, was destroyed. Among the
buildings wrecked are the royal college
and twenty.four churches. Many sugar
mills in the country are demolished,
and valuable machinery badly damaged.
In Port LOUIS alone 600 persons were
killed; in the country districts, as far
as heard from, 800. The complete
death roll is over 1900 fatalities, mostly
among the Africane, Chinese and NAL
gassys.


The roar of the gale was deafening,
and people rushed to and fro in panic
stricken confusion. Ram fell in tor
rents; the thunder crashed, and the
flashes of lightning were binding.
The authorities are making every ef.
fort to alleviate the suffering, and mill.
tary tents are being distributed among
the homeless, as IS also fOOd.


Half of the crops of sugar. rice, coffee
and pepper are utterly ruined, and the
loss is very heavy.


Although Mauritius is noted for vio-
lent and destructive hurricanes, this
one exceeds any hitherto known. Low
ering skies and falling barometers gave
warning of the approach of the storm,
and everything possible was done to
minimize the threatened damage; but
when the gale burst all the precautions
proved Of no avail. The shipping in the
harbor sent down topmasts, put out
extra anchors and paid out cables, but
80 fierce was the storm that the cables
parted like threads and the vessels were
dashed upon the coral reefs about the
island.


The horror and misery of the scenes of
destruction surpass description.

Three young girls named Maggie Brown, Ger
trude Winsor and Gertie Cox narrowly escaped
being drowned in Lake Union yesterday after
noon and were rescued only after great efforts
by Frank Latey and a gentleman who disap-
peared after the deed was accomplished.


The three girls named and Isabel Scanlon, all
of whom live in the neighborhood OF Lenora
and Sixth streets, in North Seattle, started out
for walk yesterday afternoon. and wandered
down TO Lake Union, where they came to the
Boulevard which runs along the west shore of
the lake. They followed this until
the Lake Union water-works were
reached, and here they found q
boom of logs which belongs to the Western Mill
Company. The Seaman 81 rl stayed on the planks
of the boulevard, while her companions got
down upon the logs. All went well for a short
time and the girls were in high spirits, tripping
over the logs, which lay in water about thirty
feet deep. Finally they all got on the same log
and it rolled slightly. As the girls became
frightened and tried to steady themselves the
log rolled over, and all three were precipitated
headlong into the water. Their cries were
heard by Frank Latey, who was working on a
house near by, and man who was walking
along the boulevard directly opposite where the
accident happened.


Both men rushed to the spot and after consid-
cradle difficulty rescused the girls from their
dangerous and decidedly chilly situation


Gertrude Winsor was taken home at once
The other girls were taken to Mrs. Fosters
house near by, their wet clothing removed and
means taken to avoid the danger of ill results
from the icy bath. About 6 o'clock in the even
ing tho girls were in condition to leave Mrs
Fosters and go home.

TRES PNos, Cal. July 27.-Some excite
ment attended the opening OF the land
grants today. Settlers in farm wagons
poured through the town continually

clerks Office at HOLSTER. These were

been able to prove their residence on the

Francisco land hunters who have rushed

selections, but many of whom are wait

places for settlement. Old timers are
affected very little by the opening of the
land, but the newcomers are nervous
and excited. There has been no vio-
lence, however, outside of few fights
where two settlers have located upon
the same quarter section. A few hardy
women are here to take up claims, and
will probably secure lands.

Needham opened the fight with

From the sixth to the ninth Need

contest.

Dawson now landed harder, aim

eleventh. Dawson was tired and some
what ratified and fought desperately at
close quarters. He was bleeding pro-

From the twelfth to the fourteenth

with both hands. Dawson was game,

marked, but seemed slow in following
up his leads. Dawson caught hard
| left in the nose near the close of the
thirteenth round, staggering him and

neck and chest.

shaky Australian about the ring, smash
ing him in the mouth with his left at

| appearance.

perately, and caught Needham hard
left and right on the jaw, dropping him.

despair, and drove both hands onto
Needham's head, who fell twice and
WAS all but knocked out.
| In the sixteenth Dawson landed both
hands hard. Needham was groggy, but
countered twice. Dawson dropped him
with his right, but Needham rose when
] apparently out, and the men fought
around the ring like demons. Dawson
freshened under the excitement, and
though bleeding again at the nose, was
much stronger than Needham.


In the seventeenth Needham dropped
the Australian to his knees. This round
and the eighteenth were game, but the
men were tired.


From the nineteenth to the twenty
fourth the fight progressed with vary
ing effects, but Needham was gradually
weakening.


In the twenty-fifth Needham was all
but out, Dawson smashing him on the
head and kidneys. Needham fell fiat
on his face and was down eight seconds.


In the twenty sixth Needham was
doubled up by another right-hander on
the kidneys.


In the twenty-seventh and succeeding
rounds Dawson kept up the aggressive,
feinting with his left for the head and
landing his right on the kidneys.


Needham fell six times in the twenty
eighth, more through weakness than
the blows received.


In the twenty-ninth Dawson dropped
Needham to his knees with right
on the head. Needham rushed once OF
twice, but his strength was gone. Daw
son again smashed him on the kidneys,
landing his left on the jaw at the same
time. Needham fell on his back and
was unable to rise. Dawson was de-
clared the winner.

Wordsworth and Scott both celebrated
in their poems the famous old Gelert.
This dog, a deerhound, was given by
King John to his son-in-law Llewellyn,
who kept him at his hunting lodge, in
the neighborhood of the Welsh noun
tain Snowdon. Gelert was missed one
morning from the hunt by his master.
Llewellyn, upon his return to the lodge,
saw the dog, and discovered that its
mouth was besmeared with blood. Con-
Guiding that the dog had devoured his
child. the infuriated master slew the
poor animal. Upon investigation, he
discovered a dead wolf by the child's
cradle, while the child was safely and
soundly sleeping. The brave dog had
saved Llewellyn's heir from the wolf,
A monument was erected to the faithful
creature, which bears the name of Beth
Gelert. .-Harper's Young People.

far as learned they escaped serious injuries.
The four engines were badly wrecked, the
four mail-cars are tot al loss and baggage
ear was nearly demolished. The station
agent disappeared after the wreck and ha
not yet been found.

The old fashioned corncob pipe was
not the spick and span pipe of the fac
tories, glistening with varnish and care
fully smoothed with file. The old
time pipemalker chose large and sound
cob, as nearly as possible cylindrical in
shape, cut off the lower three inches
and with q sharp penknife shaved the
outer surface down to hard, smooth
face. He then cut the bottom and top
smooth, thus considerably shortening
the piece, carefully followed the bowl,
and a reed stem placed in small hole
near the bottom completed the pipe
Such a pipe could be fashioned in q hall
hour, and it served its purpose admira
bly!-New York Sun.

A deed of quiet heroism was done

About O'Clock Mrs. Will Bulls and her

street, coming north. When near the

maddened animal would dash into a
telegraph pole. She took the little child

curb. She jumped so cleverly that she
struck fairly, and tell backward with the
little one clasped to her breast. She

afterwards the horse ran into the tele-
graph pole and Mrs. Bulls was thrown

fore she let go. She was quite severely
bruised, but was not seriously injured.
The horse, with the remnants Of the
buggy, was captured at the corner of
Eighth and Wall streets by some boys.

handsome young woman with rich

red handkerchief and from its folds took
two sticks of candy and ball Of pop
corn. The tawdry and slender stock

house who ordered the woman to move

yer from his own pocket. The sight

Nina Cnarpentler, young French
woman, was drowned at $50 O'Clock
last evening in reservoir No. 5, beyond
the end of the Downey avenue cable
line. Her violent death was the sad
ending of pleasure trip which she
went out to enjoy in the company OF her
husband and several friends.


At about 2 O'Clock Albert Charpentier,
with his wife and her friend Georgette
Billois, left the Charpentier home on
Also street for drive. The convey
ance they used was an ordinary
open buggy, to which was hitched an
ill-tempered, hard .mouthed, bucking
bronco.


The little party had agreed to meet
Almond Fercut and Paul Garatta, who
are also friends of the Charpentiers, at
reservoir No. at 4:30 o'clock, the
young men having arranged to 60 out by
the cable cars. The bronco, with the
exception OF several unexpected spurts,
behaved himself so we'll that the two
women and Carpenter enjoyed their
drive hugely.


At about o'clock they arrived at res
ervoir and found Fercat and Garatta
awaiting them. The whole party went
to the little adobe public house near the
reservoir gate, and had talk and soci-
able glass OF coda water all around.
They then broke up, the women return
ing to the buggy, and Fercat and Gar
alta starting back for the cars.


The people at the adobe house say
that when Charpentier got into the We
hicle and took the reins, the horse at
once began to back. Charpentier
touched him up with the whip, but
without effect. The obstinate beast
continued to move backward and in an
instant the whole outfit went down the
embankmenJ and into the water. At
the last moment Charpentier jumped
out of the buggy, and landed in shall
low place, the water only reaching his
waist. The horse, however, kept on
plunging backward until he suddenly
disappeared in hole, dragging the
buggy and the two women with him.


In the meantime, Fercat and Garatta
were walking over the hill towards the
cars. They heard cries behind them,
and upon turning to ascertain the cause
discovered little girl from the adobe
house running excitedly towards them.


"Come back! Come back for Gods
sake!" cried the little one. "All your
friends are in the water"


The two men at once ran back at their
best speed, and arrived at the pond Just
as Georgette Billois was coming to the
surface for the last time. Charpentier
was plunging about in the shallow water,
insane and helpless with excitement.
Mrs. Charpentier and the horse and
buggy had disappeared.


Fercat and Garatta tore off their
superfuous clothing, plunged into the
water and brought out the inanimate
form Of Mademoiselle Billois safely to
shore. Charpentier managed to rescue
himself.


The half-drowned Georgette was car
ried to the adobe and revived, while
Charpentier, realizing the horror of the
situation, tore half of his clothing off
and ran moaning and wringing his
hands, wandering up and down along
the bank. His friends had to restrain
him by force from going back into the
water.


Word was at once sent to police head
quarters and to Coroner Weldon, and
Officer Richardson and the coroner re-
sponded Mr.. Sutch of Orr & Sutch
drove out with the dead wagon, and a
systematic search was begun for the
body of Mrs. Charpentier. The horse
and buggy were discovered with a pole,
and were dragged out by team of
horses. The body of the unfortunate
woman was not, however, entangled
with the vehicle, as had been expected.


Ropes and graphing hooks were sent
for, and the search for the body was con-
tinued after nightfall from boats. The
body was found at o'clock, in forty feet
of water, and was taken to the morgue.
An inquest will be held this morning at
10 o'clock.

Another chapter of facts regarding the fatal
mtshap which befel the slave trading brig
Tahiti, in which 70 many persons persisted, has
reached San Francisco. Leon Nartel, IA Mexi-
can who has just arrived from Manzanillo,
Mexico, is the narrator. Four months ago, he
says, while up the coast of Mexico he heard Of
and visited two shlpwrecked men. One was a
Russian Finn named johnson and the other
WIS a Gilbert Islander. They told him that
they were on the Tahiti when she capsized on
October 10 last and with four Others they
escaped in boat. They had no food or water
in their tiny craft and suffered terribly from
hunger and thirst. Finally one of their num-
Der. wQnan and native Of the Gilbert Islands,
died. and for a time they subsisted on her flesh.
All the time they were suffering terrible agonies
from thirst and finally two others of their num-
Der, also Gilbert Islanders. drank sea water ard
shortly after went mad. In this condition they
plunged into the sea and were drowned. The
boat with johnson and his companion eventu-
ally drifted on the Mexican coast. where they
were rescued and cared for by fishermen. The
islander. according to the Mexican, has re-
covered from his terrible experience, but John
son was still sick when he left.

judge of the court in vacation can allow alter
nate writs of mandamus. but not peremptory
writs. 1t holds that the state board of can
vassers must base its determination solely upon
the face Of the returns. and the court there
fore strikes out of the petitions all allegations
OF matter not appearing upon the face of the
returns.


The court then takes up the demurrers to the
petitions. The Wyoming statutes require that
the county clerk take for his assistance two
justices of the peace, .'who shall canvass the
precinct returns and send abstract thereof to
the secretary of state

Double weddings are common occurrences
and triple weddings are heard Of occasionally,
but what has probably never been heard Of be-
fore took place at the farm house of James
Bunce, who lives near Stockton, Kan. This was
quadruple wedding


On the adjoining farm to that of Bunce is the
family Of William Mccoy. The two families
have long been intimate. The Bunce family
consisted of father, two sons and daughter, the
mother having been dead for ten years. The
Mccoy family consisted of Mrs. Mccoy two
daughters and one son. Mccoy died about
three years ago. t-


The younger members of the families have
been thrown together constantly, and their
intimacy ripened into love. Several times thew
have been on the point Of marriage but in
each instance they have been disappointed by
some unforeseen incident As time progressed
1t was seen that all three weddings could be
had at one time with profit and pleasure, and
arrangements were made accordingly.


While the preparations for the triple event
were in progress Mrs. Mccoy and Mr. Bunce
were thrown much together but the Younger
people were SO engrossed with their own affairs
that they dld not notice any suspicious signs
between their parents When the night Of the
triple wedding came all were ready, and the
minister called upon the contracting parties to
stand before him while he pronounced the
words that would make them united. The min
lister had been posted by Bunce and he was the
only one In the room who was not surprised
when Bunce and the widow also stood up and
joined their hands preparatory to the service


IL was not too much ola surprise, however to
prevent the young folks from carrying out
their part OF the performance, and the happy
couples are now In one united family.

SNoHoMisH. Dec. 26.-fSpecial THE
bodies of George Shoultes and Fred
Schmidt, the two farmers who were shot
dead by two young men named Robinson
and Livingstone. three miles east of Du-
buque last Thursday afternoon, were
buried in Woodlawn cemetery yesterday
at p. m. Health Officer Limerick held
an autopsy on the bodies in the forenoon.
disclosing thereby some new facts in the
affair. Three balls were found to have
entered Shoulies' body. The first entered
the back, passing through and out of the
front of the chest. The second entered at
the breastbone, coming out at the back,
just above the hips. The third entered
the left leg. Four bullets entered
Schmidt's body. any one of which
would have proved fatal All the
shots took effect in the heart. The first
was from the front through the breast. the
second from behind and through the back,
and another from side to side from one
armpit to the other. Two wounds were
found on Schmidt's left arm, and the au-
topsy showed that the heart was nearly
shot away. Several bullets found IN the
bodies of the two victims proved that
the guns were forty-eighty caliber Win
chester rifles. The supposition is advanced
that Shoultes turned around suddenly
after receiving the first shot, thus ac-
counting for his being hit both from the
front and rear.


The bodies were found at schoolhouse
a mile from the scene of the shooting,
neighbors having removed them for safety.
though the corpses lay on the ground as
they fell all Thursday night. guarded by
Deputies Knowles and Lindsay. The lat
ter stated that the bodies were twenty
feet apart when first found. Sboultes
was in sitting posture, leaning against
the branch of fallen tree, while Schmidt
was lying upon his face. According to the
best testimony Mrs. Helena Kuntz,
sister of Shoultes, was the first
person to arrive on the scene.
She states that her brother and Schmidt
started together with their axes to cut
away some trees that the elder Robinson
had felled across the road and a few
minutes after their departure she heard
rapid firing in the direction Schmidt and
Shouftes had gone and she at once started
to learn the cause. She followed their
tracks in the snow until she came upon
the lifeless bodies of Shoaltes and Schmidt.
She also stated that when the tvs men left
the house Schmidt walked a few wards
ahead of Shoultes, and that when she
found the bodies the relative positions
were not changed. There was a double
track in the snow to where Sheuites' body
was lying. and single one from there to
Schmict's remains. No signs of scuffle
appeared, and it is thought that Schmidt
and Shoultes did not know who fired upon
them and that the murderers were in am
bush and fired from the rear Both
Shoultes and Schmidt were unmarried.


Young Robinson and Livingstone are
now in the county Jail awaiting a prelim-
mary trial. which will probably take place
tomorrow.

Before registration closed number of DEM

A Fierce Fight Between Hungarian and


italian Miners.


HAzLEToN, Oct. l8.--The little mining
town of Milnesville was yesterday the
scene of race war, and as the result
ons man lies dead, two are fatally in
jured and about twenty are seriously
wounded.


Milnesville is surrounded by numer-
ous mining camps, mostly populated by
Hungsrians and Italians. For years
trouble has existed between these two
nationalities. Numerous fights have
taken place from time to time, and
number of deaths resulted, but never
before did they rise up in body to face
each other.


During the fight yesterday blood
flowed like water. A continuous fire
from pistols was kept up by
both sides, but slilettos and knives
played an important part, and were
used with telling effect. The noise of
the combat soon started the whole
mountain side, and men arrived from
everywhere. For fully 20 minutes the
work of cutting and slashirg was kept
up. How many Italians were shot can
not be told.


From Wilkesbarre comes report of
similar fight, which resulted in one man
being fatally shot. another severely
stabbed and two more badly cut, whose
wounds are considered fatal. Still an
other was fatally injured bv being bat
ted about the head with q club.

warship short distance away. The lat

struck terror to the hearts Of the Indian
crew. They Immediately hoisted all sail,
and moment later a second shot struck
the ship. piercing the forecastie above the
water line and dong considerable damage.
Then the fog again descended and the

A Long Branch express train crashed into the
rear of an Easton local on the New jersey Gen.
trail railroad at the Danforth avenue station,
Jersey City, yesterday afternoon. The rear
passenger day coach was telescoped. One
woman was badly, perhaps fatally. injured and
nine other passengers received more or less
serious injuries. The accident was due to a
delay of fifteen minutes of the trains. caused
by the Central railroad ferry boat crashing into
a transportation boat in the fog in New York
bay.


At 100 o'clock the Washington flyer. Easton
local and Long Branch express trains leave the
foot of Liberty street. A dense fog hung over
the river, and the ferry traffic was being carried
on with the usual carefulness. The Central
ferry boat had reached midstream and was
steaming along slowly, when suddenly one Of
the Central corlpany's heavily laden Transport
tation boats doomed up before the ferry boat,
and. before the engines could be reversed,
there was a terrific crash.


The passengers rushed wildly about from
side to side Of the boat and the greatest con-
fnsion prevailed. Quiet was finally restored.
and il was then discovered that the front rail of
the ferry boat had been carried away and few
windows broken.


The panic-stricken passengers were huddled
together in the ladies' cabin, shrieking and cry
ing. when the captain appeared among them
and assured them there was nothing 10 fear.


The boat proceeded more slowly to CommUni-
paw and arrived there fifteen minutes late.


The three trains were quickly made up and
the Washington flyer was the first to draw out
of the depot. Then followed the Easton local
in charge of Engineer Wolverton of Elizabeth
port The Washington train had passed Dan
forth avenue within five minutes at terrific
rate of speed.


Engineer Wolverton was running more eau
tiousy and had scarcely passed Danforth ave-
nue. when the rear brakeman discovered the
body of a woman lying on the track about fifty
yards below the station. He pulled the bell
cord and the crew hurried back to care for the
supposed injured woman. The discovery was
quickly made that the woman, who was sickly,
had tainted and fallen on the track and had not
been struck by the train.


The crew returned TO the train, which lay be-
low the depot. and the signal to start was
given. The train was scarcely moving when
the Long Branch train. in charge of Engineer
milford, rushed out of the fog, and before the
collision could be averted or warning given
crashed into the rear car of the Easton train.
The smashing Of glass and crashing of wood,
with an accompaniment of shrieks and groans,

LIVERPOOL. Dec. "A dispatch from
Kinsale. on the south coast of Ireland,
says the British steamer Lake Huron,
from Montreal. passed there this morn
ing, having in tow the North German
Lloyd steamer Spree, which sailed from
Bremen for New York November 22d,
and which is some days overdue at her
destination. The Spree has shaft
broken.


LONDON, Dec. 3.-The Spree arrived at
Queenstown this afternoon. Her main
shaft was broken early on the morning
of November Goth. Before the engines
could be stopped, the broken shaft
pounded out a portion OF the stern,
and part Of the machinery went
through the bottom under the
second cabin, which Immediately
filled with water. The passengers
thought the vessel was going to the bot
tom and rushed on deck. For time a
veritable panic prevailed, and the Off
GERS were helpless TO calm the terror
ized passengers. The water could be
heard rushing through the hole in the
bottom, and in q short time the vessel
began to settle. The widest confusion
ensued, but when it was discovered that
the vessel was not Immediately going TO
the bottom. semblance of order was
resumed. Nevertheless the passengers
were anxious, and kept life-preservers
close at hand.


The boat crews we're piped to their
stations and everything placed in readi-
ness for the abandonment Of the vessel.
1t was soon found, however, that the
water-tight bulkheads were answering
the purpose for which they were con-
structed, and though water was pouring
into the compartments beneath the sec
ond cabin, very little was reaching the
other parts OF the vessel.


When the accident occurred the Spree
was about 1000 miles from Queenstown.
Two anxious days passed, and the Lake
Huron took the disabled vessel in tow
on the 2Sth. There were 263 passengers
on board. Among them were Gen. o.
0. Howard Of the United States army,
Mrs. Adelaide Howard and child,
Dwight l.. Moody, the evangelist, Mrs
Lewis Branch and family OF Milwaukee,
DR.. Sidney Duh OF Chicago and others.


A second-class passenger named Paul
Kelson was SO badly frightened after the
accident that he jumped overheard and
was drowned. The other passengers are
all well. Some OF the passengers and
portion Of the Snree's mail will be for,
warded by the Etruria tomorrow, and
the others by the North German Lloyd
steamer Hsvel, which leaves tomorrow
for Queenstown to embark them.

tend the wedding. When she arrived the
family had gone to the ranch, but

per for the family, which returned in

after supper all the members of the family

sutferings, drank more tea. Those who
drank the most tea were sickest, and
finally doctors were sent for. They found
strychnine had been put in the tea. All
are now out of danger, except Mr.. Shaw
and Mrs. Hinkston. Realizing his criti-
cal condition, Mr.. Shaw wished to be
married before he died. and the ceremony
was performed this afternoon. Shaw is
still alive, but it is not thought he will
live.

From the New York Ledger.


The school children of Russia have recently
been made very happy by having beds put in
their bed rooms and large dormitories. In
Russia nearly all the boys at least and very
many girls are sent to boarding schools and
colleges. And SO many years of their lives are
passed in studying. eating and sleeping away
from home.


Until recently beds were quite unknown in
Russia, save as a luxury for the higher classes.
The peasants slept on top of their big bake
ovens for warmth. The soldiers slept upon
hard cots without bedding, while the middle
classes of people and the students rolled them
selves in blankets and lay down near stoves.
Recently, however, all the children in the
boarding schools and all the scholars in the
colleges have been awarded beds by special and
general agreement.


Russian children have never had cradles,
cribs, cots or beds.

She bears to Botreaux tower.

For vesper bells at Tintagel

Across the doubtful sea!''
"Fool!" sneercd the captain, thank thyself;

God pardon thee once more,


And grant that we may safely come
Unto the Cornish shore"
The captains oath was on his lips,
Or ever the sun went down,
And while the people thronged the cliffs
Above the harbor town,
A mighty wave swept DER the sea,
With dull and sullon roar;
The good ship trembled all her length
AS she sank to rise no more.
Then DER the whelming waters pealed
(As tolling funeral knells
For those lost souls) the soft, sweet chimes
OF the Forrabury bells.
The moss creeps over Boltreaux church,
Where rings no vesper lay; ,1n
Still waits the tower its blessed bells,
And silent stands today.
For low beneath the Cornish wave,


Where tangled wrecks lie deep,
The Forrabury bells are hid


And their sweet echoes keep.
But ever 'gainst the billows toss,


And storm winds shrek in glee;
Their muf1led chimes the blessed bells

with the demand.

ferior grades have entirely unsettled the mar
ket. Strawberries are arriving freely, and prices

supply OF fresh roll butter, packing has been

New LONDON. July 1.-This has been

'95's in the annual two-mile row on the

of the seasons aggregation of Yale's
athletic achievements, is the record of
the Yale's varsity eight in turning the
tables on the Harvard crew this after
noon. Criticism either of Yale's blade
or body work is difficult. The crew is
called the most perfectly drilled which
ever represented it. The Harvard oars
manship, however, was unsteady while
the stroke followed moderately well, the
inboard work of the Harvard men was
highly unsatisfactory.


All afternoon excursion trains brought
loads of people, who were soon trans
ferred to the big passenger steamers.
The water was perfectly smooth, good
breeze blowing at the back OF the crews
as they rowed down the stream with the
tide.


All the circumstances favored Yale
and adverse to Harvard. Yale chose
the east course. At SLY the boats got
off, Harvard leading with thirty-nine
stroke, Yale about thirty-eight. One
hundred and fifty yards from the start
Yale found her form and her prov shot
past Harvard. Harvard quickened her
stroke, making a fight before relin-
gushing the lead. In doing so she
dropped into bad form, causing the boat
to roll. Both crews then settled down
to a steady stroke, Harvard with a
quick, speedy dash, and Yale with de-
liberate, powerful force.


At the half mile Yale was length in
the lead, with both crews squirting. At
the mile Yale was three lengths ahead,
Harvard rowing thirty-five, Yale thirty
seven. Between the mile and the half
Yale took matters more easily and the
positions were unchanged At the two
mile post Yale was four lengths ahead
and pulling more vigorously. Harvard
was further handicapped by bad steer
ing at this point. and at the 21s-mile
post Yale was fully eight lengths ahead.
Harvard was splashing badly, the crew
having gone to pieces. After the third
milepost it was procession, Yale work.
ing with mechanical precision, with
Harvard ragged.


AS the boats passed between the long
line of yachts which enclosed the finish,
a rousing salute was given both crews
and the effect was magical. The strokes
quickened and the oarsmanehip of both
crews was decidedly more trim. At
5 :37 :48 the Yale boat shot by the finish
with Harvard fifteen or sixteen lengths
in the rear.


The Harvard's shell crossed the line
551a seconds later. Every whistle in
New London let loose and the din was
distracting. Thousands Of blue flags
floated aloft, while the crimson dropped
or kept modestly out Of sight.


The official time for the four miles
was: Yale, 20:48; Harvard, 2l :421$.

ANTWERP, Aug. 25.-The excitement
caused by the presence of Asiatic
cholera in this city is intense. Those
who can, are preparing to leave the city,
1t has transpired that the first persons
to fall victims to the disease were dock
laborers. They were taken to hospitals,
where the doctors, though they were
probably fully aware that the disease
was Asiatic cholera, stated to newspaper
representatives that it was common
cholera, and nothing was to be feared
from it. They acted on the worn out
theory that the concealment Of the dis
ease will prevent its spread. That
their reasoning was fallscious was
soon proved, for other patients
were soon brought to the hospital, suf-
fering from the same disease, and the
number of cases has constantly in
creased since. The first victim died
almost Immediately after entering the
hospital, and the appearance of the
bodies, if nothing else, was sufficient
proof that common cholera had not
caused the deaths. The bodies retained
their heat for longer period than is
usual when death is caused by another
disease, and looked as though they had
been through long attack Of sickness.
Many physians hold that post mortem
examination would have developed the
fact that malignant, and not simple,
cholera was the cause of the deaths.

Mrs. Louisa Stoker was taken to the Re-

She had tainted from hunger at the corner

At the hospital che quickly rcgaIned con-

around her light blue eyes. She was at

"My last meal" she said, was cup OF

weeks | have eaten but little. and during

Mrs Stokes was not strong when her
money gave ont, and when illness came to
make her poverty more unbearable she be-
came frantic.


Her father is Edward Ftsimmons, a
rancher of Vallejo She came to this city
about two mouths ago and began 10 look
for work. She was about % years old.


She had married, but for years had been
separated from her husband. When she
left him she went TO her fathers house,

She might have remained there, but she
preferred to earn her own living. She had

SACRAMENTO, March S.-Just after the
polls closed this evening in the irst pre-
cinct OF the first ward, "Big Neck"
Smith, San Francisco ward politician,
shot and killed Patrick Brannigan, a
plasterer OF this city. The latter was
considerably under the influence Of
liquor. He and Smith had little quar-
rel earlier in the day, and Brannigan is
said to have threatened to kill Smith.
When they met this evening some words
passed between them on the sidewalk,
in the midst of crowd, when Smith
drew big pistol and shot Brannigan
twice, and as the latter fell upon the
sidewalk Smith placed the pistol to his
head and shot the third time. Branni-
gan died instantly. The deceased leaves
a wife and five children. He was ma
tive of New York, and in his younger
days was prize fighter of some note.
Brannigan had made no demon
stration at the time he was shot.
After the first shot, however,
he tried to draw pistol but dropped
his hand when shot the second time.
Smith surrendered TO Officer Gibson
and was marched to the police station.
Much indignation is expressed and
Brannigan's friends talk of taking Smith
from jail and lynching him. Smith has
been making his home here for some
time. He was very officious about the
polls today and had several quarrels
with citizens.

rous victims in the London Whitechapel

caught the next train and reached Washington
q few hours after the couple arrived there.

Of the young girl.

LONDON, Jan. 31.-There was rioting
in Eastbourne today, caused by the Sal,
walton army holding a special celebra-
tion to commemorate the founding OF
the corps. After the usual morning SER
vices, the Salvationists marched through
the streets under police protection, and
were disturbed only by running COM
ments and chaff from the crowds on the
sidewalk.


In the afternoon mob rapidly col
lected at the Salvation army citadel, and
as the soldiers filed out, they were SUBJ
jected to more chaff, accompanied by
the singing of ribald parody, yelling
and hooting. Several hundred well
dressed men formed corps twenty
abreast and were followed by the army
to the beach, where it was proposed to
hold meeting. Along the whole route
windows, balconies, and even car
riages in the streets, were filed with
citizens and visitors watching the scene.
A huge mob awaited the army at
the sea front. The police had great diff
fculty in clearing the way for the SOL
diers, who had to cling tenaciously to
their instruments and flags, without
daring even to attempt to play note.


As soon as the service began, the mob
swept down upon the army, shouting ::
'Throw them into the sea-" The forces
of the police were augmented and they
behaved in most creditable manner,
resisting rush after rush, although
nearly overpowered by superior num-
bers. The Salvationists were pelted
with pebbles by their foes through the
hour.they remained on the beach.


When the service ended the members
of the army commenced the return
march. They climbed to the parade
with the utmost difficulty, their assail-
ants making frequent rallies, but failing
to capture the Salvationist flag. Des-
perate hand-to-hand encounters with
the policemen were continued. A few
clergymen and soldiers were present,
but held aloof.


When the struggling crowd reached a
point opposite the Burlington hotel, the
police having become exhausted, an
other rally was made and proved sue
cessful. The flag was seized and torn
into shreds. Caps were torn from the
heads of Salvationists and tossed into
the air or kicked into the roadway.
Some frail-looking lasses swooned from
pain and fright and were nearly tram
pied upon. The scene of violence was
continued till the army retreated into
the "citadel," and even then the mob
was 10th to disperse, and still came into
collision with the police. Several Sal
vationsts were badly injured and their
uniforms were all spoiled.


PARIS, Jan. 3l.--A band OF members
of the Salvation army met with highly
hostile reception on the Boulevard des
Italiens here today. There were num-
ber of scuff1es between roughs and Sal
vationsts. A mob encouraged the as
saults by kissing and hooting the har-
rassed band.

VroroRrA, B. c., May 30.-TSpecial. +
The crew of the steam schooner Challen-
ger reached here tonight on the Alki from
Alaska. They report leaving Sand Point
last October for Boring sea. arriving at the
Island of st. George in the middle of No
vember. When they reached there they
landed and dubbed hundreds of
seals under the walls Of the
guardhouse. Russians sent around
natives to inform the patrol, and in the
rush back to the schooner one of the boats
was capsized in the surf and five men were
thrown out, but subsequently rescued.
The natives had the struggling
men in the water covered with
rifles, but the officers forbade
them to fire and allowed the
men to get back to the schooner. The
next night when hove to off shore storm
sprung up and the vessel was completely
under water for several hours, the
decks were swept clear, the FORE
wrecked. After the storm the schooner
reached the Aleutian islands and pro-
ceeded to Makitat. Here they disposed of
tH0 SkluS, kettlng al OIuer Oh inc Alaska
Commercial Company for their money,
and proceeded to Unalaska to get the Or
ders cashed.


On her arrival the deputy United States
marshal and customs officer, with the COM
mander of the Rush, boarded her, and
finding eight more men on the
ship than on the articles and
having also suspicion of her
business, detained the schooner and sent
her to Sitka under arrest, giving her coal
and provisions, out of which the crew
had run. The stores were placed on deck
and swept away on the first day out.
The crew for two weeks was almost
starving, and again managed to reach
Unalaska. where their statement of the
reasons for their return were disbelieved,
and the owner, mate and chief en-
gineer turned states evidence, describing
the raid on the island. The crew were then
sent to Sitka under guard and various
sentences were imposed in the Sitka court.
The men finished their sentences
last week, but the captain Is
still serving his. While in Jail tho
men were visited by Major Williams,
who filed 500 pages of foolscap with seal
ing information from the thirteen men,
who now say they filled him with fairy
tales as literally as be had filed them with
good American whisky.

One Of the most terrible scurvy-ridden

The ship was the Hawaiian Isles and

She was given up for lost by many.


The Hawaiian Isles was in command of

According 10 the captains report she

From June to had strong head winds,

The state in whit h the ship reached port

In its most violent form, and two OF the

In the first place, the vessel behaved very

The men seemed in bad health from the

When Cape Horn was reached there was

MEMPHIS. March 9.-Four Deputy Sher-

In grocery-store gang OF negroes entered

Others. 1t Is believed, will recover. On

shot from revolver crashed through

The Chesapeake and Potomac Telephone
Company appeared before the District Comis-
sioners yesterday and called their attention to
the fact that an act Of Congress approved two
years ago permitted the company to lay twenty
miles of underground wire. By an act Of
March, 1891, the Commissioners we're directed
to prevent the construction of more than five
miles of sub wires for telephone service until
April last, unless Congress should first pass
some general law on the subject of underground
conduits, based upon the report OF the electrical
inspector.


Congress having failed to pass such law the
company contended that the fve-mile limitation
had expired, both in fact and in spirit, and that
their permit had thereby been revived. The
company informed the Commissioners that they
had under the old permit made extensive ar
engagements with view of establishing gen.
eral underground system; that its main Lines
have been constructed in different directions.
and that unless connecting lines can be laid and
they be allowed to complete the system con-
templated they will lose the money invested in
building the main lines.


Without expressing any official opinion the
Commissioners referred the matter to the attor-
ney for the District for his opinion.

LONDON, Aug. 15.-The British ship
North, Captain Newson, at Sligo from
Portland, Ore, reports that on June
11th, in latitude A degrees south, lon
gitude 81 degrees west, she passed two
enormous icebergs, while many more
were visible ahead. The North sailed
north with solid ice barrier of bergs,
ranging from twenty to 200 feet in
height, while the open water was
filed with great quantities of broken
ice. At 10 O'Clock on the night of June
11th the vessel was entirely sur
rounded by ice, and it was feared that
she would be crushed, but, fortunately
toward morning the winds changed and
enabled her to clear the bergs. She had
many marvellous escapes from destruc-
ton. The berg formed a breakwater
fifty miles long, resembling large vol
canic island. This report of the North's
bears out reports from other vessels
from around Cape Horn that the ice
drift from the Antarctic ocean this sea-
son is unprecedented, and that it has
reached the most northerly point ever
known.

was rather weak, owing to liberal receipts. Val.
ues had to submit to reduction in consequence.
Apricots and peaches are in great abundance,
and quoted lower. Berries of all varieties sell
slowly, and there is little inquiry for them.
Choice red nectarines are in good demand and
steady; white varieties neglected. Apples and
Bartlett pears are plentiful and bring fair val
ues.


In the dried fruit market, the demand is con-
fined to apricots. Aside from this there is
little doing.


The vegetable market was overstocked with
all kinds and values are weak, with downward
tendency. Potatoes and onions, especially
common red, are dull, the latter practically
unstable. The supply of green corn, summer

Mrs. Hope, of Luffness, who died re-
Gently in her eighty-first year, was a
link with the long distant past, for she
was granddaughter of the Lord Doug
las who obtained world wide fame as
the winner of the Douglas case, which
was perhaps the most extraordinary and
romantic litigation on record. Lord
Douglas, the successful claimant, had
one daughter, who was the heiress of his
vast possessions, and she married the
younger brother of the fourth Duke of
Buccleuch, who was created Lord Mon
tagu of Boughton, and who is now only
remembered through his friendship with
Sir Walter Scott. Lord and Lady Mon
tagu had three daughters, of whom the
eldest married the late Lord Home, and
she inherited the Douglas estates.


Mrs. Hope, who was the youngest
daughter, married Mr.. George Hope, of
Luffness, some time Tory member for
Windsor, and brother of the famous
James Hope Scott. Mrs. Hope died at
Boutwell, Castle, Lanarkshire, which had
been her principal residence for many
years past, and she was buried in the Luff-
ness vault at Aberlady, East Lothian, the
funeral being attended by the Duke Of
Buccleuch and Lord Home and by nu-
merous members of their respective fam
ilies.-London Truth.

His Yacht Alva Sunk, But His Own Life


is Saved.


Boston, July 24.--The steamer III. F,
Dimock, of the Metropolitan Steamship
company, arrived this evening, having
on board the occupants of w. K. Van,
derbilt's yacht Alvs, which the steamer
ran down this morning.


The Alva, under command of Captain
Morrison. left Bar Harbor at 4 O'Clock
Saturday evening, bound for Newport,
K. L., having on board the owner and
his guests-Frank W. Vanderbilt, Geo.
De Forest, Louis Webb, Winfield Scott
White and Frank Riggs-all OF whom
are esummering at Newport.


Early this morning thick fog set in
and Captain Morrison deemed it i'm
prudent to run further, as Che yacht was
in the track of coasting vessels. After
making Pollock Rip lighthouse, anchor
was dropped. Whistles and horns were
blown at frequent intervals.


Shortly after q. m. the guests were
aroused by heavy crash, accompanied
BIZ the tearing of the plates of the ves-
sci. William Vanderbilt was first on
deck. Looking through the fog they
could see the dark hull of a large steam
er, backing away from the yacht. The
yacht hailed the steamer, and informed
the captain that the yacht must sink.
A steam launch, four row boats and a
naptha launch were lowered from the
Alva, which was rapidly sinking, and the
owner and passengers, with the crew OF
fifty-two men, were soon rapidly pulling
away from the doomed craft. The exit
was none too coon, for when they were
about cables length from the vessel
she plunged down, bow first. and moth
ing but the tops Of three masts remained
above the water.


The Dimock was going at greatly re
duced speed when the collision occurred,
otherwise she would probably have run
right over the Alva, and frightful loss
OF life would have been the result
owing to the fact that all the passengers
and half the crew were asleep at the
time of the accident.


None of the passengers or crew saved
thing except their clothing. The
Alva was one of the finest pleasure
steamers afloat, and cost nearly half 6
million dollars. Efforts will be made tt
raise her.

the fittings. The damage will not neces.
state the ships return to Mare Island
