New YORK, March 1.-The present aer-
ial disturbance is due to the meeting of
two storms. one of which came up the
coast from Carolina, the other having its
birth in Central Ohio and going East.
Each increased in violence until they met
about midnight last night. Vessels COM
ing into p?rt through He'll Gate report
terrific weather on the sound, all being
delayed and all the passengers aboard
vary sea sick. Atlantic Highlands, n. j.,
reports the highest tides ever known.
Considerable wreckage has been
cast ashore. A large vessel is
reported wrecked of Sandy Hook.
Several hundred feet of the
new railway were washed away near Mil
ton Park and a large pile-driver sunk in
deep water. This morning, on Staten
Island, the tide was the highest ever
known, and had it risen another inch all
the apparatus on Ellis island would have
been rendered useless. The furnace rooms
of the big immigration buildings were
flooded this morning and it was only by
the greatest efforts that the fires were kept
going. The upper bay was filled with
wreckage today. One of the Staten Island
ferries passed the wreck of a canal-boat
drifting near Oyster island fiat. A
large number of smaller crafts are
reported seriously damaged, and there
was much difficulty experienced by
ferry passengers il boarding and departing
from the beats. Many piers were sub
merged by the high tide. In the city
many telephone and telegraph wires were
blown down and poles broken and wrecked,
and there was much delay in transmitting
messages.


The storm is still raging furiously to-
night, the surf at Long Branch having
torn away twenty feet of the bluff in front
OF the old Leland hotel, and great damage
is threatened by the high tide tonight.
From Elberon to Seabright strong surf
is tearing out the beach badly,
and partially completed bulkheads
are all demolished. Several cot
tages near the coast are in danger. The
storm is tearing out all the wires along
the coast, and has carried away the pipes
Of the Long Branch water-works, cutting
off the water supply of the cottages at
Monmouth Beach and Seabright At At
lantic City building in course of erection,
intended to be one of the finest business
structures in the city, was blown down
and several smaller buildings demolished.
The storm is also raging through Pennsyl-
vania.


READING, Pa, March IA violent wind
storm, accompanied by rain, snow and
hail, passed over this city this morning,
lasting two hours. Damage was done all
over the city and surrounding country.

near the CITY

Two Emperors.


KEEL, June THE arrival of the Russian
imperial vessels at Kiel was favored by perfect
weather, not cloud being visible. Besides the
merchantmen which were lying in the harbor
twenty-five German men-of-war were at
anchor there and every vesse, was
gaily dressed with flags. When the
Polar Star, flying the German military flag at
the foretop, passed the feet. she was greeted
with a deafening cheer. The sailors manned
the yards and the German bands played the
Russian national anthem. while the band on the
Polar Star played the German anthem.


The Polar Star came to anchor opposite the
castle between the Hohenzollern and the Ger
man ironclad Beowulf. which is commanded by
Prince Henry of Prussia, the emperor 8
brother.


Before coming ashore the car, attired in the
uniform of the German Alexander regiment,
visited the Hohenzollern. He was met at the
gangway of the yacht by the emperor, who
wore the uniform Of the Russian regiment of
which he is colonel. Their majesties embraced
and kissed each other three times
Then they descended to the emperor's state
room, where they conversed for twenty min
utes. The car then returned to the Polar
Star, on board of which he was shortly rejoined
by the emperor. After another cordial inter-
view their majesties landed and proceeded to
the castle.

San FRANCISCO, Dec. 1.-Two fisher

Berkeley shore while the southeast gale
was raging. For two hours they clung

was close at hand, tired nature gave out
and they fell back into the bay. The
men were Gustine Faulconi, owner of
the boat, and Luigi Morrizes, his assist
ant. 1t waa predicted on Tuesday after
noon that the storm had passed and that
clear weather was to follow. Early in
the evening the two men started out to

nearly capsized the boat. The frail
craft was rocked about like a chip and
big seas poured into her. The entire
night passed and the boat got no farther
Than Goat island. In the morning she
was overturned and the men were
thrown into the bay. They were both
good swimmers and managed to climb
onto the bottom of the boat. The
waves Wasne0 over Gnem again ana
again, but they clung to the keel with
desperation. Ihier clothing was heavy
with salt water and thier fingers were
numbed with cold. They could hang on
no longer and slid from the bottom into
the bay and were drowned.


Antoine Martino was caught by the
gale and narrowly escaped with his lie.
He went out on Saturday night and was
caught in the gale. On Sunday he was
driven ashore on Sheep island and there
he remained until rescued yesterday.
When picked up he was more dead than
alive, as he had had nothing to est for

LONDON, Feb. 21.-The latest dis
matches from Ireland say the snow-storm
continues. Traffic on the railway lines
IS greatly interrupted. Several trains
are embedded in huge drifts.


The snow-storm in Ireland continued
throughout Saturday night. All trains
on the Waterford and Limerick system

resumed today. The Limerick and
Kerry line is completely blocked. A

losses of live stock.

boat was seen keel upward, but her crew
could not be seen, except two men, the
first of these clinging to the boat in
desperation. He was seen to be twice
washed off. The second was swimming
in an effort to reach safety. The efforts
made by the coast guard to help the
men proved too late and both were
drowned. Two boats from the wreck
and quantity OF wreckage have come
ashore.

A Norwegian schooner, disabled by

town today. Two of the crew are sup
posed to have been drowned.

into Queenstown today. Her crew were
drowned. and the vessel was found aban-
doned off the head.

Adriatic and Umbria have arrived from
New York. Both were unable to touch
at Queenstown ON account of the gale.


BARKENTINE STRANDED.

Patric is stranded at Alkalow rock.
Three of the crew are drowned.

Some nights ago Bill Benchoff and

dozen dogs and two boys to carry the
pine torches. A coon was raised on the
east side of the Monterey, and the dogs

ing around underneath. The boys

away at what he thought was the coon
but no animal tumbled.


Yingling in the meantime had been
tearing paper and trying to ignite a
match, but it was damp and would only
splutter. Benchoff was deriding him
when suddenly great ball Of fire illu-
minated space. Yingling had succeeded
in igniting his match and was emptying
a roman candle into the tree.


The first ball struck a branch and
burst and the second hit the coon
'plumb CENTER" Its fur caught fire
and with yell it came rolling down
among the angry dogs. The third ball
revealed two more coons in the tree, and
Benchotf's rifle dropped one, while Ying-
ling, with the last ball in the candle, hit
the limb on which the third coon clung
with pitiful terror, and it lost its hold
and tumbled into the mouths of the
waiting dogs.


They got six more coons that night
with the help of Yingling's candles, and
now the colonel regularly shoots the
romans and Benchoff shoots the gun.

ers in all the region. n.-Gettysburg Pa.)

DEL MONTE, CAL, Jan. 16.-The San
Francisco Press club spread itself today
in the entertainment of delegates to the
International League of Press clubs,
The Southern Pacific company furnished
special train, and at 8 O'Clock this
morning party OF nearly 200
left San Francisco for Monterey.
A stop was made at Palo Alto
where carriages were in waiting and
took the party to Senator Stanford's
stables. There all the equine celebri-
ties were exhibited. Then the visitors
were driven to Leland Stanford, Jr.,
university, where they were received by
President Jordan and shown through the
college, after which they took the train
and quick run to the Hotel Del Monte
was made. After lunch the hotel party
was driven over the famous seventeen
mile drive, to Cypress Point. The
weather was beautiful and the
guests returned to the hotel
charmed with California. In the even
ing hop was given in the hotel ball
room. Tomorrow morning the delegates
will visit Santa Cruz, the big trees and
San Jose. Monday they go to Mt. Ham
ilton to inspect the great Lick telescope.

Fire broke out on the fourth floor of the ten
ement house No. 236 East 29th street, New
York, yesterday at noon. The building is mar
row, five stories high and without fire escapes.
On the fifth floor lived Henry NJ. Knoblauch
with young son and his pretty sixteen-year-
old daughter, Katie. A few minutes before
the fire started Katie returned from o visit to
Mrs. Bernard Byrnes and brought back with
her the latter's two children--Mamie, two
years old. and Stella, four years old. When
the alarm was given Katie appeared at an open
window. Taking little Mamie in her arms, and
looking down as if measuring the distance,
which was over fifty feet, she cried:
For Gods sake catch this" Then she
let go. and the baby, turning over and over.
went down with awful speed. The baby missed
and fell on the stone tagging.


Katie soon appeared again at the window
with little Stella in her grasp. Leaning out OF
the window she took her little charge by the
hands, and letting her hang down as far as she
could, shouted, Catch her!" With q loud
shrek she released her hold and Stella fell. In
her descent she struck the top of show win
dow on the second floor and then dropped into
the arms of George McFadden.


Katie herself was the next. She held to the
window sill and tried to get footing on top
Of the window below. George Mccormack
pulled off his overcoat, and Thomas Corners,
John Smith and Edward Welsh each took hold
of q corner and pulling it taut waited for her
fall After hanging for several minutes she let
go. Down like shot she went. and striking
the top of the show window she bounded into
the coat with SO much force that it alnos,
slipped from the grasp OF the strong hands that
held it, Her head would have struck the pave
ment but for Minnie Hentz.


An ambulance was called and at the hospital
the surgeon found that Katie had only suffered
slight cut On the right leg. Little Mamie
Byrnes received severe injuries. One thigh
bone is fractured, her face is cut and her body
bruised. Her sister Stella is suffering from
Commissions. the chief of which are about the
face and neck. Her jaw is also broken.

LONDON, Jan. 2.-Telegrams have
been received here from Congo which
confirm the statements made by Father
Ohrwalder. He said forty Europeans
are still in the hands of the Mahdists at
Ondurman. They are loaded with man.
acles and cruelty beaten. In telling OF
the mode of life while in captivity
Father Ohrwalder said the Mahdi
granted no provision for the sustenance
of captives, but allowed them sufficient
liberty to earn living as best they
could. Father Ohrwalder lived by tail
oring and weaving, and the sisters by
baking and selling bread. During the
last eighteen months the fugitives lived
in mud huts, but previously their only
shelter was made with their own hands
from cane and maize stalks.


They describe Khartoum as all de-
stroyed, excepting only the Austrian
church and General Gordon's palace,
and they say vegetation is covering the
sites of the houses. During two years
famine and smallpox made fearful
ravages in the Soudan. Maize rose to
ten times its normal value. but now
food is plentiful and cheap.


Today's advices from Congo corrob-
crate Father Ohrwalder's report of the
waning power of the dervishes in
Southwestern Soudan. They state that
frequent conflicts occurred between the
Mahdists and the native chiefs, and the
latter were often victorious.


Father Ohrwalder and the sisters
travelled direct from Korosko to Cairo
and dispatch received from the last
named city, stated that the priest in
speaking of affairs in the Soudan, had
said the numerous widows OF the Mahdi
are complaining that the Khalifa Abdal-
lah does not provide them with main
tenauce befitting their stations, and that
their grievance had been supported by
the Khalifa Ally Sherf. The latter also
oppose Abdallah's scheme of making
the mahdiship succession hereditary,
instead OF as provided for by Mahomet.
These dissensions are weakening the
power OF mahdism, and Father Ohr-
walder says the people would welcome
any chance to relieve them from its
tyranny.

received here from the Congo which con-
firm the statements made by Father
Orhwalder. He said that forty Europeans
were still in the hands of the Mahdists
in Omdurman. They are loaded
with manacles and cruelty beaten.
In telling the mode of living while in
captivity, the father said the Mahdi
granted no provision for the subsistence
of the captives, but allowed them sufficient
liberty to earn living as best they could.
Father Ohrwalder lived by tailoring
and weaving, and the sisters
by baking and selling. bread.
During the last ten months the fugitlves
had lived in mud huts, but previously
their only shelter was made with their
own hands from canes and maize stalks.
They describe Khartoum as all destroyed
excepting only the Austrian church
and General Gordon's palace, and vegeta-
ton is covering the sites of the houses.
During two years famine and smallpox
made severe ravages in the SOudan. Maize
rose to ten times its normal value
but now food is plentiful and
cheap. Today's advces from the Congo
corroborate Father Ohrwalder's report of
the waning power of the dervishcs in the
southwestern part of the Soudan. They
state that frequent conflicts have occurred
between the Mahdists and native chiefs,
and the latter have been often victorious.


Father Ohrwalder and the sisters trav-
eled direct from korosko TO Cairo, and a
dispatch received from the last named
city stated that the priest, in speaking of
affairs in the Soudan, had said the
numerous widows of Mahdi are COM
planning that khalif Abdallah
does not provide them with
maintenance BETTING their station, and
their grievance has been supported by
Khalif Sheriff. The latter also opposes
Abdallah's scheme of making the Mahdi's
succession hereditary, instead OF elective,
as provided for by Mohammed. These
discussions are weakening the power of
the Mahdi, and Father Ohrwalder saws
the people would welcome any change to
relieve them from its tyranny.

Steamer Lucy Lowe was burned near
Deception pass about O'Clock Monday
evening, with a cargo of 200 barrels OF
lime she was taking from Roche Harbor
to Tacoma. The sea was very rough when
she entered the strait outside the pass,
and. being heavily loaded. she shipped
water. causing the lime TO slake and set
fire to the vessel. She was out about
mile at the time, but the captain ran her
in on the beach, and she was entirely con-
sumed. None of her crew was injured.


The matter was kept rather quiet for
some reason and the 6rst information re-
earding it here was in dispatch received
by Captain Bryant, local inspector OF
hulls. from Supervising Inspector Lub-
book. of San Francisco, yesterday. 1t is
probable that Captain Jordan, master of
the vessel, telegraphed the news to her
owners at San Francisco, and from
them it reached Captain Lobbuck.
Captain Jordan ard six other mem
bers of the crew came In on the
steamer Wasco last night, but none OF
them could be found. therefore the only
information that could be received regard
ing the disaster was that gathered from
the crew on the Wasco.


The Lucy Lowe was about the most sea-
worthy boat on the Sound. She was built
for freighter, and after being engaged as
such on the Sound for some time, was
fitted out as wrecking vessel and spent
the greater part of last year in wreckng
cruise along the upper coast. Business
became slack in that line and during the
winter she came back and engaged in
carving lime from Roche Harbor to Ia
coma, taking back such general freight as
she could get.


The total loss was probably about 81, 200
to $1,000, of which 81 200 was on the cargo
and the balance on the vessel. 1t Is
thought the vessel was insured


The following dispatch from Port Town
send gives the details of the burning of
the steamer:


PoRr TOWNSEND, April 6.-lSpe cial 1.-The
steam schooner Lucy Lowe was burned TO the
waters edge near Fidago City early on Monday
morning. She loaded l,2j0 barrels Of lime at
Roche Harbor Sunday night and sailed
for Tacoma. Heavy seas flooded the decks
and the lime slaked. The deck load was thrown
overheard and the vessel headed for Deception
pass, when the cargo in the hold was found to
be on fire. The engineers and firelnen were
driven from their quarters, and the fiSe spread
rapidly. Steam was only kept up by the crew
rushing down through the binding smoke
and shoveling coal into the furnaces anG
returning TO the deck. Before the vessel could
reach the shore the flames drove the captain
and officers from the pilot house. The steamer
was scuttled in two fathoms of water, and as
she sank the boilers exploded. The crew had
gotten safely ashore in the meanwhile


The Lowe was owned by the Commercial Com
pany OF san Francisco and was valued at $40, ZOO,
partly insured. She was formerly British
sealing vessel, which was captured in Bering
sea FIVE years ago, confscated aud sold by the
government

Guillarde, an Italian laborer, today shot
and fatally wounded his wife and
brother-in-law, Jacob Canada. and then
killed himself. The Guillardes lived
near Telegraph hill. and the husband
had always been hard-working man,
but rather Eighty at times. No cause is
known for the crime, and it is supposed
he was insane.

Guillarde, this afternoon, when Gull
larde rushed in and fred two shots from
revolver at CANADA. Both shots
took effect in the head, and
the man fell unconscious to
the floor. Guillarde then fired two
shots at his wife, one striking her in the
head, and the other missing. He then
struck her with the revolver several
times, stunning her. The madman
then fred a bullet through his own
heart. dying instantly.


Canada and his sister were removed

The latest invention credited to an
American woman is ball dress cover
ing, intended for those who must walk
to the scene of festivity. This ingenious
woman had her cloak made in very
light silk finished waterproof, like a
deep bag gathered into two bands. This

buttoned round the waist. When the

text:
Three People Killed Under the Grant


Monument in Chicago.


CHICAGO, June 16.-Three persons
were killed, two seriously injured and
some forty more stunned bya fash of
lightning which struck the Grant mon
ument in Lincoln park, tonight.


The killed are: Lewis Meyer, Mrs.
Shelby and an unknown man.


The injured are Harry Phillips and
Mrs. Matte Olson.


The catastrophe was the result OF
severe electrical storm, during which
the people who had congregated in the
park took refuge in the vaults under the
monument. The storm began with
slight shower, which rapidly devel-
oped into asmall hurricane, accompanied
by the downpour Of rain, vivid flames Of
lightning and terrific peals of thunder.
When the storm was at it's height, q
binding flash struck the, statue, TAX
ing a course directly through the little
crowd underneath. Everybody, with
the exception of three men, vas thrown
from his feet. None, however, suffered
further injury than a severe stunning,
with the exception OF those named.


The lightning did not strike the
bronze figure of Grant. and the damage
to the monument will be covered by a
few dollars.

RosLYN, Sept. Especial. l-Another
fatal accident occurred in the new slope at
the Roslyn coal mine today. Joseph
Erman was killed and Charles Jones was
seriously, if not fatally, injured. At
O'Clock this morning the force that had
been at work during the night boarded the
first trip out, as was their custom. As the
trip neared the entrance to the stone the
speed of the cars was so rapid that the en-
gineer was signalled to stop them. For
some reason he failed to respond, and all
of sudden the wire rope hauling the trip
parted. Most of the men jumped off the
car, and escaped unhurt. as the trip started
down the slope at lightning speed.


Erman and Jones were thrown from the
cars, the former falling beneath them.
Before the cars jumped the track the trip
had reached the first bullwheel down the
slope: The body was removed and a
coroner's jury impaneled. The inquest
resulted in finding the engineer. Carter
Nichols, and the rope rider, Edward Pres
tage, guilty of negligence. No warrants
have yet been sworn out for the arrest of
either. Erman was single, but Jones has
a small family.

NEW WESTMINSTER, April 20-[Special
Edward Gleneross, eldest son OF the pro-
prietor of the Queens hotel, left for the
South today, taking with him Miss Florrie
Scott, pretty young girl of Is summers.
Young Glencross, who is only year or
two older than the girl, had evidently COM
pleted all the arrangements beforehand,
but they were nearly knocked endways
by an uncle of the intended. The couple
met on the ferry steamer Surrey, intend
ing to cross to South Westminster and
take the Great Northern railway for Seat
tie. The uncle, however, got wind of what
was happening, made his appearance on
the steamer and crossed the river with
them, using all the arguments he could
think of to induce the girl to abandon
her design, but without avail.
Fearing his sweetheart might be detained
by force, the ardent young lover hired a
horse and carriage which was on the
steamer, and when the ferry reached the
landing Miss Scott jumped into the buggy
and drove down the road a short distance,
Glencross holding the uncle in the mean
time to prevent him following. When the
buggy was sufficiently distant Glencross
broke away and, putting on good racing
pace, was soon in the buggy along with
his intended bride, and minute or two
later the rig bearing the happy couple dis
appeared down the road to Blaine, where
it is believed they will get married.

PORTLAND, April 20.-George W. Dress
ler, a veteran of the Mexican war, was run
over and killed today by passenger train
on the Portland & Willamette Valley rail-
way. The old man was walking across
the trestle at Elk Rock, near this city, when
he saw the train coming. He stepped off
the track onto bent, but before the train
reached him it is supposed he fell back on
the track. Both legs were cut off and
dropped down into the gulch below. His
abdomen was badly cut and his entrails
strewn along the track. Deceased was
employed at the Qswego Iron Works.

Disappearance of the Only witnesses OF


the Champion-Ray Killing.


DOUGLAS. Wyo., May ga decided
sensation was created here this morning
by the sudden disappearance of the only
known witnesses against the cattlemen
who are now prisoners at Fort Russell.
Just before the invaders attacked the
X. @. ranch they captured two
trappers named Jones and Walker who
were held prisoners until Champion
and Ray were killed, and then released.
Both made their way to Casper, and on
Wednesday last were brought here and
placed in charge of Deputy Sheriff
Kimball. The men claimed to have wit
messed the killing of Champion and Ray,
and as matter of fact were the only
living witnesses who could testify posi-
lively against the regulators on charge
of murder. Kimball went to Glenrock
last night, leaving deputy in charge,
and when he returned this morning
Jones and Walker had disappeared.
The men were allowed to run about town
during the day and slept in the office OF
the jail. Both came in late last night,
apparently pretty drunk, and
about midnight went out "for
a walk" leaving the deputy asleep.
Search was made for them and tele-
grams sent in all directions, but
no clue as to their whereabouts has yet
been received. The fugitives carried
away two revolvers belonging to the
sheriff.

LONDON, Aug. 26.-There is no doubt
that cholera has at last entered England.
The disease was brought here by the
steamer Gefma, which arrived at
Gravesend yesterday from Hamburg.
It was reported the steamer was in
fected, but the authorities, after exam
lining the passengers, allowed them ta
land. A few hours afterwards, two
aliens, who arrived on the Germa, were
taken sick. They were at once removed
to the hospital at Gravesend, where
doctors pronounced their malady chol-
era. In spite of medical aid, they both
died shortly after being admitted. This
has caused considerable anxiety, and a
close inspection Of all In coming vessels
has been ordered.


The report of two deaths from cholera
at Gravesend was telegraphed through
out the country, and produced great ex-
element today. The steamer Laura,
plying between Hamburg and Lynn,
arrived at Lynn. The officers found
two cholera suspects on board, and the
vessel was Immediately ordered to put
back to sea. The officers and passen-
gers protested against such summary
treatment, but the health officers were
obdurate and refused to let q single per-
son LAND from the steamer.


Sixty passengers on board the Ham
burg-American steamer Columbia, from
New York, which arrived at Soutbamp-
ton yesterday, changed their minds
about proceeding to Hamburg, when
they learned that the cholera epidemic
prevailed there. They left the Column
bia, when they found the company had
ordered that she proceed no farther, and
took passage for Flushing, in the Neither
lands.


Prince Esterhasy, an attache of the
Russian legation, has been suffering
from an attack of the disease known as
cholerine, but is recovering.

houses are subjected daily to rigorous
inspection to see that they are kept

complied with to prevent the introduce

text:
Great was the commotion when she ap-
peared in the morning with the evidence
of having slain seven coons, and she has
been a hunter ever since. Her father pre-
sented her with double barreled shotgun,
and she is an expert in its use. She is also
fearless rider, well educated, quite good
looking, and not a bit masculine in appear
ance. But she naturally loves coon hunt
ing. One night she fell into quagmire
and had to send her dogs home for help.
Twice she has been severely bitten and
scratched by co6hs, the last time about a
year ago.


One night she heard u racket in the hen
house. Thinking that coon had got in,
she arose, and taking lantern and her
brothers. ball club went out to dispatch
the animal. The farm hand had forgotten
to close the door of the henhouse, and Lena
found it wide open. The chickens were
still restless, and going to the door the girl
held the lantern over her head and looked
in. AS she did so monster coon attempted
to run by her through the door. The girl
struck at the animal and hit it, but did not
disable it. AS she raised her club to deal
it another blow it sprang upon her with
such force that she staggered back, and
striking her heel against stick she fell,
with the coon scratching at her throat.


Protecting herself as best she could with
her arms the girl called for her father
who came running from the house with a
gun. The coon, undaunted, kept gnawing
and scratching at the girls arms Her
father did not dare to attempt to shoot the
animal for fear of killing his daughter,
and clubbing his gun he knocked the coon
from the girls body and the animal es-
capped. The girl was seriously hurt this
time, and she was obliged to lie in bed
three weeks before her wounds healed and
she recovered her strength.


She makes good deal of money from
the skins, and has made herself magnifi-
cent hunting dress of tanned coon hide,
elegantly trimmed. In this she is said to
dazzle the eye as splendid Diana of New
New England.

Della Keegan was her name. She was
fifty perhaps, and years of dissipation had
reddened her nose, whitened her hair, made
loose folds and wrinkles under her eyes
and drawn deep lines in her face.


Still she had never fallen so low before
as to be arrested and spend night in the
station house with females worse than
herself.


So, when she stood before Justice Ryan
in a New York city police court that morn
ing, she trembled and clutched the iron
railing desperately. She had been put out
Of the wretched little room which she oc-
cupied in a big tenement house on West
Fortieth street-been thrown out on the
sidewalk while drunk. The woman of
whom she had hired the room had come to
the police court to see that Della was pun
ished to the utmost extent of the law


II have never been arrested BEFORE"
said Della in a hestating, scared tone.
Then the other woman told the justice
that Della had been put out of several
places for drunkenness.


''Three MONTHS" said the justice.


AS Della heard the words she put her
hand to her head ana sank noiselessly to
the floor.


Come, carry her out" said the rounds
man in charge of the court squad, and
five policemen pick upthe fainting woman
and carry her back into the pen, where
she comes back to painful consciousness
all too soon, and the wheels of Justice
move on without break.

Special to the HERALD


TUNNEL CAMP, near Redlands, April
30.-At O'Clock this morning the
water was turned into the new tunnel
which is being constructed by Prof. S.
Leonard Of Los Angeles for the Bear
Valley Irrigation company, from the
plans of Chief Engineer Taylor. Over
700 inches of water was running through
the tunnel all morning, and distributed
to the thirsty fields towards Moreno,
Aleasandro and Perris. The great i'm
portance of the tunnel is shown by the
anxiety with which the ranchmen
watched its development, and the Joy
with which they greeted this, it's first
trial.


The structure is half mile in length
and is over three times as long as that at
Olive. 1t penetrates mountain about
halfway between Redlands and Ales-
sandro. All the water for this end OF
the San Jacinto valley will go through
it. The water comes from the Mentone
mountains, eighteen miles from this
camp, and arrives here from its source
in forty-fve minutes, as clear as crystal
and as cold as ice.


The construction of the tunnel has
taken remarkably short time consider
ing the many Interruptions to which the
work has been subjected. During
the progress of the tunneling the
water supply depending upon the
structure for transit has been
limited, and periodically there would
come large and violent kick
from the ranchmen. In these instances
the Irrigation company has been COM
PEELED to interrupt Contractor Leonard.
Such an interruption begins today, and
700 inches. of water will run through the
tunnel for one week. The force of men
employed here have almost all left tor
Redlands, San Bernardino and Los An
geles.


A week from Monday the water
will again be shut off, and work
will be resumed. The entire
tunnel is already foored with cement
concrete, topped with cement plaster.
The side walls are of brick masonry, laid
in cement mortar, and are finished with
cement plaster. The whole tunnel will
be arched over with brick, and when
completed will have clear aperture OF
6% feet.


Chief Engineer Taylor, Supervising
Engineer lie Comte de Musiere and the
officers of the company have inspected
the work and are highly pleased with it.

The Grand Army of the Republic has ended
its encampment, and the veterans OF many
battles as they return to their homes among
the sixty-fve millions of people to whom they
have given united Nation, are watched with
admiring gratitude in every car and street.
Americans are not a demonstrative people,
They do not often break out into wild hurrahs
when their deepest feelings are stirred. But
the chances of respect and honor, the eyes often
dmmed by grateful emotions, which greet the
heroes of thirty years ago wherever their Ia
milar uniforms and well-remembered badges
are seen, tell of stronger regard than the
passionate outbreaks could express with which
men of other races might greet their bene'
factors


TO these men, and the larger army of COM
rades who have found rest, the Americans OF
this day owe the most powerful, most pros
porous and most united Nation on earth. 10
them we owe the grandest pages OF the New
Worlds history. To them we owe deeds OF
devotion and heroism which live forever to
make the American character devoted and
heroic. To them we owe tho worlds knowl-
edge that American smartness and thrift
in business, and eagerness for material
success, nave uOb lllduO Jul POVPAS
of the grandess moral achievements 10 these
same veterans the Nation owes more than a
quarter of century of such growth and pros
perty as no other country has ever enjoyed so
that already tho youngest of the family Of great
nations Is the richest and most powerful. All
the blessings that now delight u.s. all the price
less blessings that we hope to transmit to the
generations coming after us, come to the
Americans Of to-day through the self-sacrfcing
patriotism and bravery of those who wear the
blue. When their deeds are no longer remem-
bered and honored by Americans, then indeed
this people will be unworthy Of its priceless
heritage


In the mellow moonlight. of distance 1t may
seem an easy and simple thing for these vet
Grams to have marched to the defence of their
Government But they left industries and
business and earnings behind them. Most OF
them left behind happy homes, and loving wives
and tender children for whom they would have
given their lives. and when they marched away
at the call of duty they knew that many who
went would never return. They faced death
on the battle field, and still more deadly dis
ease. With full and strong ranks they marched,
but when they returned the flags were torn and
the ranks thinned and distant graves held many
of their number. 1t was grand thing that
these men did and the grander for their lofty
motive-that sef-government should not perish
from the earth-and great have been the results
which those now realize who honor these vet
Grams for their fidelity.


Honor waits for them while any OF them live.
Nothing that thankful people can do will be
too much for those who rskcd all and gave
all Well may hearts beat more quickly and
proudly when Americans remember their ex-
ample and their deeds. Well may the people
rejoice that so many Of these heroes are yet
with us, to kindle by their very" presence the
noblest patriotism.

Choked by Her Own Hair.


A highly sensational story comes from Brook
lyn regarding the death Of Miss Lillian Nor
folk, adopted daughter Of George H. Norfolk Of
Flatbush and Franklin avenues, Flatbush, Mon
day night. Early yesterday morning she was
found kneeling dead beside her bath tub. her
hair caught in the faucets. An hypothesis has
been advanced that she committed suicide,
either from love or dependency, but it finds
little credence.


Miss Norfolk's physician told the coroner that
she had been drinking whisky very hard lately.
He thought that she had become i'll while lean
ing over the bath tub and had toppled over, her
hair C'beautiful golden tresses," according to
one account, and craven black locks" accord
ing to another) becoming entangled in the
faucets and twisted about her neck choking her
to death. She did not have strength or intelli-
gence enough to disentangle 1t and so she died.


Miss Norfolk was one Of the best known
young women in Flatbush society. She was q
member of the Amaranth and Gilbert Societies,
and entertained her friends in lavish style.


From her youngest years she had exhibited
talents and action out of the ordinary run, and
was fond Of dramatic speech and gestures.


As an amateur actress she had gained quite q
reputation before her mother died, two years
ago. This last mentioned event seemed to have
changed her usually merry disposition greatly.

Considerable CONSERVATION was caused
yesterday afternoon at Kerkow's New
Vienna Buffet by good-looking and
well-dressed young Mexican woman,
who was evidently looking for gore. She
drove up to the ladies' entrance at about
8 o'clock, and took a seat behind the
screen which separates the women's
tables from the body of the house. She
was dressed in plain black, and carried
with her silk umbrella and hand
some riding-whip with finely carved
ivory handle. Her manner was excited,
and as she waited at her table her face
twitched convulsively.


She looked desperate enough to do
almost anything. To a HERALD re-
porter who talked to her, she appeared
almost frenzied. She said she was
looking for a man who had wronged
her, and, when urged, gave the name of
a wealthy and we'll known man about
town as the individual upon whom she
desired to wreak her vengeance. When
asked her name she declared that she
was one of the 'Three Minnies" of Mex
leo city, and then went off into wildly
passionate denunciation of everything
American. After several hours wait
ing, during which she amused herself
with eccentric behavior, the young
woman entered her cab and drove off,
without having satisfied her thirst for
blood

WARSAW, May 14.-Josephine Giriich had the
reputation of being the most beautiful ballet
girl in Warsaw. She was the craze among the
Polish nobility. both young and middle aged.


A few days ago the town was shocked by the
announcement that Josephine Gerlach had been
found murdered. Her disordered attire showed
the clutch Of bloody hands. The finger marks
left by the murderer were not large. but rather
slight and indicated to the police that woman

called upon Josephine. Searching inquiry

police did not hesitate to arrest her. They

her happiness and fhe resolved upon revenge

visit, and watching her opportunity, struck her
with the hammer. The girl attempted

time breaking her skull and Draining her. She
then stabbed her repeatedly with the dagger

ing recovered consciousness. His wife, Au-
gusta, is convalescing and will, in all proba-

the Jewish faith, but was Of the Catholic per-
suasion and attended church regularly. He
had been married three times, Augusta being
his third wife. When his second wife
died he had two children, his first wife's,
and in order to provide for the children he
took unto himself the third wife. The children
soon became dissatisfied, and in order to keep
peace in the family the father took them to
Germany. Some five years later he returned
here, bringing one child, Tessie, and opened
the cigar store 1245 It'll street. Seven months
ago, when he was getting along nicely, the wife

began, resulting Saturday in the tragic death

ing an inquest unnecessary.

MARsHFIELD, Ore., Sept. 27.-After 10
days of suffering from cold and hunger
and the probability of filling watery
grave, Captain O'Brien and his watch
man, William Holmes, were rescued
from the whaleback steamer Wetmore
this afternoon, by Captain Bergman
and the Umpqua life-saving crew. A
week after the crew had been taken off
the wreck, Captain O'Brien and his
watchman went aboard the vessel dur
ing a calm to prevent parties from
boarding her and claiming salvage. A
storm came on, and for the last 10 days
all the efforts of the liie-saving crew to
rescue the Hhipwrecked men were futile,
and it seemed certain that they must
perish. The sea was not running 30
high today as yesterday, yet it was a
hard struggle for the rescuers to reach
the vessel. After several hours work
they put a line aboard, which O'Brien
and Holmes tied about their waists, and
then jumped into the sea. The life crew
pulled them safely to shore.


The men were almost worn out from
starvation and exposure. For the last
five days they lived upon a scant meal
day, and this morning they divided their
last biscuit. Their suffering from cold
was terrible, and for two days they have
atood in water up to their waists, with
the spray dashing over their bodies.


The wharf at Empire was crowded to-
day when the men came ashore, and the
greatest interest in caring for their wants
was taken by the citizens OF that place.


The weatherside Of the Wetmorsae
main cabin is stove in, and the vessel
will undoubtedly prove total loss.

The wonderful feats of East Indian
jugglers have formed the theme of many
letter from travellers in the orient, but
none are more surprising than that for
which an old sea dog, now lying at the
water front, vouches. While he was an
officer on board the P. and o. steam
ships two natives came aboard at Mad
ras, he says. They were juggler and
his assistant. After they had performed
number of minor feats and gathered
quite a crowd around them they called
for a sack and piece of sailcloth.


These having been provided the chief
juggler made small tentlike structure
with the canvas and some stools. He
then placed his assistant in the sack and
allowed a sailor to tie the knot which
bound him fast prisoner This done,
the chief carried the sack into AN open
space, warning the people to stand back
some distance, and then carried on an
animated conversation with his assist
ant, whose replies could be distinctly
heard coming from the sack. Suddenly
the chief rushed forward, picked up the
sack and dumped it overheard, where,
to the horror of the passengers and crew,
it sank out of sight.


Immediately the captain rushed for
ward and seized the man, under the full
belief that he had murdered his compan-
ion, but the juggler only smiled, and
pointing to the canvas, asked that it be
raised. This was done, and the sup
posed drowned man was discovered
squatting on the deck. So realistic had
been the throwing overheard, however,
that it was some time before the sur
prised passengers could realize murder
had not been committed.-New York
Evening Sun.

staggered when they read eighteen and two
tenths

rick place. mile below Where It is only

San Francisco, Aug. 12.-The brig
Galilee arrived today from Tahiti and
Marquesas islands, bringing further
particulars of the murder of the crew OF
old King Pomare's yacht and the subse-
uuent capture of the murderers. After
the king Of Tahiti died his yacht was
sold, and was loaded for trading voy-
age.


The mate, named Rodegue, and his
his brother, were the only white men on
board. After trading some time the
brothers took the vessels cook into their
confidence, and all the others on the
vessel were poisoned, their bodies
thrown overheard, and the vessel put
for Kings Mill island.


The cook had quarrel here with the
brothers over money matters, and in
formed the authorities of the murder.
The Rodegue brothers were arrested and
placed aboard British man of war, and
together with the cook, were removed to
Tahiti.


At the time OF the capture of the
yacht, the vessel had aboard sixty tons
of copra, one ton of pearl shell and $4,000
in cash.

WASHINGTON CITY, Dec. 24.-The presi-
dent has called upon the treasury depart
ment for oil the information in its posses
sion relative to freight coming into the
United States over the Canadian Pacific
railroad. The unjust discrimination
against United States railroads, made by
law. or rather by its construction in favor
of the Canadian Pacific by means of the
consular seal system, has long been a
source of complaint in the treasury de-
partment. Under this law freights are
shipped from Canada 10 interior points in
the United States under the consular seal
system. The United States consul certi-
fies that the manifest is correct. that he
has sealed and closed the car. and this
certifcation carries freight through with
out Inspection at the borders, thus saving
from one to two days delay and the
cost of rehandling freights. etc. When the
law passed traffic was small, but gradually
business has grown until, instead of
handling only Canadian goods in this way,
the law has been prevented and now more
goods having their origin in China and
Japan are shipped over the Canadian Pa
cilc through the United States than
goods from Canada. Furthermore, the
Canadian Pacific managers have had
duty of 10 per cent. placed upon coffee
and tea coming from the United State.
into Canada, while the same articles from
other countries are free. The effect of this
mas been to divert this traffic from Ameri-
can ports and have coffee and tea come
over the Canadian Pacific from Fancou-
yer, b. C. This evidence of unfriendli-
ness is regarded at the state department
as requiring some drastic measures. 1t is
therefore proposed 10 suspend the opera
ton OF said section until congress shall
make proper provision to stop discrimina-
ton AGAINST American RAILROADS.

EDITORS HERALD: So much has been

the so-called old board that l wish to

They came into power when the shell

victions for any criminal offense were
few and far between, and when the
streets were in horrible condition, all of
which they have righted, and today the
little town is the most orderly, criminals
and disorderly characters being ban
ished, and we have the finest graded
streets and sidewalks and more miles of
them than any place on the coast for it's
size.


Our public library and reading room
is the finest, also, on the coast.


They secured for Santa Monica the
wharf that the Southern Pacific will
commence to build, and the coming of
the Santa Fe by their wise and liberal
policy.


They also brought about peace be-
tween Jones & Baker and the town,
thereby securing the valuable esplanade
which will shortly be turned into the
finest park in the world.

"A desperate fight among three China
men took place at an early hour yesterday

Is In laundry at the corner of Washing
ton and South Sixth streets. He awoke

ike demon to get away, and in the melee

hnally the lamp was overturned. In fall
ing it went out and left the terrified
lighters in darkness.

rived with light bloody spectacle met

Washington, October 5.-Ihe two naval

which our navy will be the first to adopt.

feet than any smoke stacks on naval or mer-
chant ships, with the single exception of the
English merchant steamer Scott, which has
adopted the high Ign, stack These ., new t stacks,
draft and give additional draft in ordinary
steaming, by reason of the increased force
with which the smoke viii be drawn through
the high tunnels. Another advantage looked
for, is that all the smoke and gas will he car
ried clear of the marine tops and not Interfere
with the men there in working Calling guns
and light fire pieces The pro-
posed towering tunnels through which
the volumes of smoke will pass will not add
any to the grace and beauty of the vessels,
but rather detract from their appearance.

text:
The poet Whittier has his home in sum-
mer among the foothills of the White
mountains, and in one of his local songs
he writes,


Through Sandwich notch the west wind sang


Good morrow to the cotter;


And once again Chocorua's horn


OF shadow pierced the water.


Chocorua, which can be seen from the
poets home, is tall mountain, perfectly
bare on top, and bereft of all vegetation.
There is native legend in connection
with it, as with all old Indian
localities, that is very interesting.
Chocorua was the chief of a great tribe
who dwelt on the borders of what Whittier
calls ''his broad Lake Ossipee." For years
the tribe and their mighty chief were SUI
preme: but one day the white man came.
The strange visitors had conquered all the
other Indians. but Choeorua was bound
not to submit For days and days the
battle ragged, until the chief alone was left,
and he fled from the conquerors. The
white men followed him on and on,
pressing close behind, until the chief sped
up the rugged mountain side and left
his enemies below. Then he raised his
hands aloft, and prayed to the Great
Spirit to grant his hnal wish; and
he cursed the mountain on which he
stood. and ordered nothing to grow upon
the summit while the white man held the
land. Long and hard was his curse upon
the mountain top; and when he had fin
ished, night had come, and the chief
leaped into the darkness and vanished
from sight for evermore. And, runs the
legend, from that time forth the noun
tain was called Chocorua, and the curse of
the old Indian was fulfilled, for today it
is bare and bleak. Such was the story
told one summers night beneath the
shadow of the mountain just as the moon
outlined it against the sky.

The sheriff's officers with the aid of
civilians yesterday afternoon captured
two Mexicans named Chas. Ramon and
Paulo Rendon for stealing grain from
Dick Garvey's ranch. Garvey has been
missing grain every season for three
years. Yesterday morning Foreman
Garner of the ranch again missed
twenty-six sacks of grain, and upon in
vestigating discovered the tracks OF
wagon leading from the granary.


The foreman trailed the wagon, and
near the Leguna rancho overlook the
two Mexicans mentioned. They had
the stolen grain in wagon. Garner
tried to arrest them, but they would not
submit. He therefore rode back at top
speed to get assistance. In the mean
time the two Mexicans threw the barley
off the wagon and drove off toward
Lugo. Garner overlook them again
with his companions, and Rendon
jumped from the wagon and escaped.
Ramon, however, was captured.


The foreman then telegraphed to
Sheriff Gibson, who sent out Deputies
Bowler, Russell, Barham and Charles
Cruz to assist Deputy Sheriff Brookshire
OF Downey in the chase of Rendon. At
noon the squad got saddle-horses at
Lugo and circled aroung among the will
low patches surrounding the spot where
Rendon had disappeared. They searched
all afternoon, and as sundown ap-
preached were about to give up the
chase, when suddenly Deputies Russell
and Bowler came upon the grain-thief
hidden in a willow bush. Rendon
started to run, but was halted by the
fash of a gun.


Both prisoners were brought to the
city and locked up in the county Jail.

A Southern California vaquero per-
formed remarkable feat in San Fran
cisco recently. While riding his mus
tang he suddenly came upon runaway
team. The vaquero rode close to the
animals and, bending over until he al
most touched the ground, caught the
reins, which were trailing. There was
sudden evolution Of man and beast,
and the brave mustang stopped as though
shot. Its hind legs were doubled under
its body, its forelegs were extended and
Jose sat erect with the reins of the
team wound tightly around the horns Of
his saddle. AS the reins drew taut there
was prodigious jerk, tearing of the
pavement under the broncho's stubborn
feet, a swapping of harness, and the big
horses, checked in their impetuous rush,
were thrown to the ground and cap
tured.-Exchange

WEST PoINT, Miss, April 6.-The
most stdestructive stolm that ever visited
sthissssection is VOW prevailing. The
rain which has fallen constantly for four
days, eliminated last night in regular
waterspout from Greenwood to the
Alabama line and from Macon
to Corinth. The streams are
all overfowed and many bridges
have been swept away. Miles of rail-
road track are submerged, and many
miles of roadbed destroyed. On the
Georgia Pacific four miles of track have
been washed away, and in this county
the loss of bridges alone is enormous.
The rivers are higher than ever
before known, the water covering
the country for miles around. Many
houses have been washed away, and
several colored families have been
drowned. At Aberdeen the water COW
ers several streets and the people are
greatly alarmed. 1t is still raining.


MEMPHIS, Tenn, April 6.-Dispatches
from Grenada, Carrollton and other
points in Mississippi, state that it has
been raining hard for several days. The
rivers are out of their banks and great
damage is being done to railroads and
other property.


STORMS IN ARKANSAS.


BRINKTRY, Ark, April 6.-The wind
and rain storms that have for the past
two days been prevalent in this dis
trict have caused great damage to prop
erty, and in some cases injury to per-
sons. At Carlisle, small station west
of here, one life is reported to have been
lost, and several persons seriously in
jured, in the cyclone OF yesterday after
noon.


A CHICKAsAW TOWN WIPED OUT.


DENIsoN, Tex, April 6.-The report
has just reached here that Owensville,
small town in Pickens county, Chick
asaw nation, was wiped out by
a cyclone Sunday night. Two per-
sons were killed outright and several
injured. Every house in the village was
leveled. The clerk of Pickens county,
Chickasaw nation, was probably fatally
injured. His team and vehicle were
caught in the cyclone and hurled
through the air. There is no telegraph
or railroad connection with the town.


NORTHWESTERN STORMS.


ST. PAUL, April 6.-Monday's storm
was heavier and more general in South
Dakota than at first reported, but nc
casualties have been reported. The
rainfall at Huron was nearly three
lncnes, the greatest ever known at one
time in April. Reports from various
parts of the state, also from Nebraska,
Iowa and Minnesota, indicate that Hu.
ron got the heaviest rain, while other
localities were visited with more or less
snow. West of Huron and extending
into the Black hills country the fall ol
snow was five to seven inches, and very
heavy with water.


CYCLONE IN NEW YORK.


CLEAN, N. Y, April Ga terrific cy'
clone struck this city last night, wreck
ing ten houses and a church. One
woman was killed and a number of peo'
pie seriously injured. There were six.
teen people in the church when struck,
which was carried twenty feet away.

What can be more pleasing than the
unmolested edge of an old road, where
hazel and elder hang out their fruit for
the birds, where the fragrant clethra
blossoms, where the wild grapevine and
the glossy bramble climb from tree to
tree, and wild roses and morning glories
brighten the shadows with their smiles?
Here in the spring the trientalis and
anemone make the ground beautiful
with their white blossoms, while the
shad bush waves welcome to the passer-
by. AS summer comes the sky blue

and the epilobium show pink and purple
amid the foliage, the mullen lifts its
stately yellow blossoms from its furry
leaves, while barberry shows first its
arcs of yellow bloom and later it's coral
clusters of fruit that contrast well with
the great goldenrod and the splendid
purple of the wild aster in the fall

text:
She Was Going Away, and All of Her


Friends Remembered Her.


She was going to leave home on an
extended visit, and her friends began to
hint of various little gifts of remem-
brance which they would magnani-
mously bestow upon her departure She
beamed gladly and looked at her old
gloves significantly when her brother
said something about goodby present.
Her old purse, too-oh, she wouldn't be
humiliated by its loosened clasp burst
ing open at just the wrong time and re-
vealing its vast emptiness Moreover,
she wouldn't experience any more con-
gestive chills when her last dime slipped
behind the tattered lining, and the con-
ductor fidgeted while he moved his lips
just as If he were rehearsing that por-
ton of the street railway bylaws in
which no one is entitled to ride except
upon the payment of the nickel fare.
Her calling cards also-surely some one
would remember that she was now Miss
Smith. since Sister Sue was married.
And Mrs. Browningl Didn't she sigh
out to every one she met that her whole
soul was in turmoil over an un-
Quenchable desire for volume of these
poems?


Well, about week before she left the
first package arrived.


"It's just the size-it must be the
pocketbook," she cried joyfully. $50
soft, too-what beautiful leather it must
be! A place for small change and one
for bills-rll stuff that full of cotton to
make it look full-and a pocket for
cards, I'm sure"


But, To-! Upon disclosing the contents
there lay two handkerchiefs.


''Oh, WELL" she sighed, trying to be
optimistic; sit isn't so bad after all, for
the initials are pretty"


Following that every mail and every
caller left little bundles of various di-
mensions and degrees of softnegs and
weight, and each time she opened them
with eager fingers, while visions of en-
graved pasteboards, fresh purses and
dainty poems rose in transcendent glory
before her expectant eye. But, alas!
nothing but little linen squares till her
handkerchief box ran over and flooded
her whole dresser with waves of snowy
linen.


"Do they expect me to have contin-
ual attack of Influenza" she cried in
sheer desperation as particularly
promising parcel evolved into series
of pink, blue and cream squares.


She seriously contemplated following
the example of the young men of Har-
ward, who drape their windows with
curtains made of handkerchiefs pur-
loined from their various girl friends;
she even dreamed of being smothered
under the loads of odious things, and
glared SO savagely at the old washer
woman, who came home with profuse
apologies because zone O. them handker-
chiefs got lost somehow" that the poor
creature fled in fear.


At last she was at the station, and she
gave sigh of relief that she could not
possibly be attacked by any more hand
kerchief fiends. She was just settled
in the car, with magazine on the seat
Browning, and she had contrived to
tuck her tattered purse down in her
jacket pocket with her tipless gloves,
when papa handed over little package
with;


"Here, my dear, it's little, but l
wanted to give you something"


She waited until they got out into the
country, where the fresh air and the
feeting green and gold of the landscape
vrould revive her, when with trembling,
half hearted haste she gingerly united
the string And there lay two handker-
chiefs!-Chicago News.

SEATTLE, WASH, March 30.-The
steamer Macarthur, of the United States
coast and geodetic survey. was sunk at
the coal bunkers this evening. She was
loading coal with all the ports on the
berth deck wide open. The coal came
in more rapidly than was expected, list
ing the boat to port until the water
rushed through her port holes. Before
anything could be done to right her she
went down. The vessel was towed q
few yards nearer shore as she was going
down, in the hope that she might land
high enough to be partly out OF the
water when the tide goes out, but it is
thought she landed over rock ballast
pile, and it is possible that she will
break in two when the tide goes out.

SAN Francisco, March 30.-A New
York special says: 1.-The peach crop
killers are sending out fresh alarms re-
garding the prospecte of the coming
season in Maryland and Delaware. They
affirm that the late storms and cold
weather have done more or less damage
and that there is not chance for any
thing like full crop. Some estimate
that 80 per cent of last years harvest is
all that can be calculated upon from the
present outlook. Others guess that it
will not be over 20 per cent of the aver
age crop; still others 60 to the extreme,
prophesying only 10 per cent of the
average crop. The stories are generally
credited here. Meanwhile canned
peach spectators are making hay
while the sun Shines"

aries; lions, elephants and hyenas

Hunter, alias Todhunter. in February last,

ring and gold bar brooch with three jew
els in it. One of the witnesses. Mrs.

Began wore jewelry exactly similar several
days before her arrest. The police cannot
discover what has been done with this jew
elry. and the fact of their making away
with it tells heavily against them. The
case will not come on trial before July.

Miss Maud Walthew, q very pretty
young woman of 20 years, was painfully
injured and permanently disfgured by an
elevator accident in the Seattle National
bank building yesterday afternoon at 1
O'Clock.


Miss Walthew is student at the Queen
City Business college, which is on the Sec
ond floor of the bank building, and at
Duncan, Miss Corinne B. Leland and Miss
Anna Church. she took the elevator for
the sixth floor, where the girls daily have
singing exercises. When the elevator
reached the sixth floor the elevator boy.
Charles Hammond, aged about Is years,
was inclined to be facetious. and
would not let them out. Miss Walthew
took young Hammond by surprise, and,
unsnapping the door, stepped out, but the
other girls were still held prisoners. The
elevator door had no glass in it, and Miss
Matthew put her head and shoulders
through into the elevator car and in a
moment more would have opened the door
and liberated her companions, but the boy
gave the hydraulic lever shove and the
car dropped downward few feet. Miss
Matthew made an effort to withdraw her
head and shoulders, but was not quick
enough, for the upper portion Of the car
caught her just above the eyes and
her mouth was forced against the
lower edge of the casing with
such force as to tear away the cedar pam
els. Her nose was broken and her cheek
bones injured, while the flesh was torn
from her face and the nasal bone forced
downward into her mouth. Her head
would have been severed from her body
had not the casing given way and allowed
her head to be pushed beyond reach of
the car


As soon as the elevator boy saw the in
jury he had done, he ran the car quietly
to the sixth floor level, opened the door.
and before the terrified girls inside could
recover from their terror, sprang out and
ran away. He has not since been seen.

fessor T. II. Dining, of the college, and
]. p. Amspoker, one Of his pupils, carried

home at ILL Fifth street. Mrs. DR.. Dean
and Drs. Goodspeed and Palmer were
called and attended to the injuries. In q
few hours she was resting easily. and,
though terribly disfigured, she is likely to
recover.

mess college for the rest of the afternoon.
The girl is very popular and was con-
sidered the life Of the school. She showed
much spirit during the painful operation
which followed her removal to her home,
and her only thought seemed to be Of the
grief caused her mother and the rest of the
family

ization's Constitution.


INDIANAPOLIS, Dec. PA conference
of the Populist leaders of the country
was held here today. The central OBJ.
ject was to further the organization OF
the farmers secret political body known
as the Industrial Legion. About 25
states were represented. Chairman
Taubeneck of the Populist's national
committee and Paul Vandervoort, head
of the Industrial Legion, were both
present. The meeting made sweeping
amendments to the constitution to meet
Vandervoort's views, who refused to
lead it under the present constitution.

body were done away with. Its charac-
ter will now be purely political, and it
will join hands with the Peoples party.

mander-in-chief, the only military title
retained. Vandervoort says the object
of the organizations secrecy is to keep
spies out of camp, and that the order
already numbers 100000 members.

The Psyche butterflies appear

To rhythms of some thought divine.

OTTUMwA, Iowa, May 22.-Fifty armed
citizens cut the levee at this point to-
day to save their property from destruc-
ton by the continually increasing flood.
The water company, whose property was
injured, appealed to the mar
shal, but that officer was powerless
to overcome the determined men. The
superintendent of the water company
endeav0red to check their intentions,
but withdrew when revolver was lev
elHd at his head. The levee was soon
cut in three places, allowing the water
to escape. Additional houses and barns
were swept away. and while no lives OF
persons were lost, cattle and horses were
carried away.

order to advance was given this morn
ing, and the troops at once moved to

vessels began to hurl shells. The efforts

grand assault on the works, and

rebels, TIE troops carried the fort.
In the meantime the gunboats we're
bombarding Fort Santa Cruz, and so
effective was their work that the rebels
were soon forced to surrender. The
troops eventually obtained possessionso Of
all the forts which had been seized, and
the prisoners were again placed in cells.
The firing during the attack on the fprts

places of business and securely bolted

-Four men struggled for their lives on
a burning tug three miles from shore

dawn. The men were the crew of the
tug John A. Miller, suddenly aroused to
find the engine house mass of flames

steam on the boat was headed for the
shore, but the rapid fire drove the
wheelsman from the pilot house, and
then the blazing and unmanageable tug
plowed the choppy waves in great cir
Gle, the flames swiftly eating their way
to the stern, where the four men stood
helpless against the fury of two ele-
ments. They had fought the fire till
almost exhausted, their hands and faces

m every direction for sign that help
was coming.

Welcome saw the flames of the burning
boat The throttle was thrown wide
open, and the little boat, with the
whistle footing hope for the imperiled
crew, plunged through the heavy sea
toward the burning tug. Blazing al
most to the waters edge it was running
mad race through the waves. Two
brothers of the Welcomes captain were
on the burning boat, and, in danger of
collision or of catching fire, the We'll
come shot after the Miller on its course.


1t was a thrilling race. Round and
round the boats went before the We'll
come could touch the Miller. The four
men crouched astern. The flames leaped
toward them. They were scorching the
faces of the men. With squirt the
Welcome crushed into the Miller Three
pairs of arms shot out over the bow
and in a moment two of the four

Another squirt and the rescuers managed

New York, Feb. CIV. E. Ferguson,
of the New York produce exchange,
recognized authority on statistics on the
grain export trade of this port, has just
made his annual report. The tables
compiled show an enormous increase in
the grain export trade Of New YORK, and
dwindling away OF the American ocean
marine, the American merchant flag be-
ing driven off the seas by Great Britain.
The completeness with which steam has
superseded sail in the ocean carrying
trade, may be seen from the fact that
of 1888 vessels which carried cargoes of
grain from this port during '91, only
fifteen were sailing vessels.


4 There was shipped from New York
during 1891, 6S, ,223 ,528 bushels of Amer
lean grain to feed the hungry mouths OF
Europe. Not included in this were $780,
377 bushels of buckwheat, which APP
pears in the statistics for the first time,
buckwheat never having been exported
before in any quantity.


OF 1888 ship loads only twenty-five
were carried under the American flag.
There were only four American steam
ers left in the grain-carrying trade
three old passenger steamers of the late
American line, which used to run from
Philadelphia, under the control of the
Pennsylvania railroad.


Great Britain has the lions share of
the worlds carrying trade, and no less
than 1872 shiploads left this port under
the British flag last year.

MARsEILLEs, May 31.-Mails which have
just arrived from Mauritius confirm the
statement that 1900 persons we're killed and
1000 injured in the recent hurricane. The
wind was preceded by violent magnetic
disturbance. The sea rose nine feet, the
highest level since the cyclone of 1918.
Scarcely a house in the colony escaped
damage. Many churches and public build
ingS were destroyed. The church of the
Immaculate Conception is in ruins. The
cathedral by a strange chance escaped. The
dead include large number OF the leading
inhabitants. Fearful sights were witnessed

estate collapsed, killing 200 Indians. Half
Of the sugar crop is destroyed and the plant
erS' losses are incalculable.


About noon the storm broke with a
furious kissing sound, and for 80 minutes a
pitless tornado ragged, accompanied by a
deluge of rain. Buildings collapsed, roofs
were blown off and trees blown down. The
barometer suddenly began to rise, the wind
lulled. and many people went out, believing
that all danger was passed. At 8 o'clock
the wind burst again in tenfold violence
frcm the directly opposite quarter. The
fury was maintained for two hours. At 6
O'clock the weather again became calm, and
fires then broke out in the eastern suburbs
and destroyed what the wind had spared.


The country districts suffered heavily, but
as nothing compared with Port Louis. Here
the residents who survived the disaster
we're almost too daZed and unnerved TO be
of much assistance in the work Of restoring
something like order out Of the state of
chaos which existed.

CHICAGO, June 21.--A circus tent
greatly magnified, with dozen huge
white pendants stretched from the GOV.
ering to the floor, was the appearance ol
the big Democratic wigwam today.
. What appeared to be pendants, were
really stout posts, supporting q great
canopy of wood, raised some distance
above the walls, to admit light and air
from all sides. Blue silken banners
we're distributed on the main floors,
bearing the names of the various states,
and showing where the state delega-
tions should be seated. Around and
back of them, rising like an amphi-
theater were eleven tiers of seats for the
spectators. The entire structure has
room for more than twenty thousand
people.


The chairman's desk, the same over
which Tilden and Hendricks were
nominated in 1884, was surmounted by
huge bouquets of flowers. Today the
great interior was wreathed in red,
white and blue shields OF the different
states, with portraits of honored Demo.
Gratis of the past. The states were
seated according to their alphabetical
order, Alabama having the front row,
New York being we'll back.


The crowd began to gather as early as
IL o'clock, though the convention was
not to be called to order till noon, and it
was long after that hour before the actual
calling to order took place. When the
gavel finally fell, the great structure was
completely filed with people.


While the convention was assembling,
the blue satin banner of the Horace
Boies club OF Davenport, Ia, was borne
forward at the head Of that delegation oi
rugged men who will sit in the conven.
ton and vote for their governor to the
last ditch. They were greeted with ap-
plause. as were the Tammany leaders oi
New York, who followed closely. Then
came Illinois and Pennsylvania; then in
groups, pairs and singly, the other states
took their places.


THE CONVENTION IN GLOOM.


It was high noon. A black shadow
crept up from che north and overspread
the sky. The great spaces under the
galleries became dim and shadowy. A
hush crept over the throng, and white
faces were turned upward to the open.
ing beneath the light wooden roof.
Was the roof again to be blown away
Would the terrific winds come out of the
growing blackness? Was there danger
Would there be peril in remaining?


But as the shadow finally enveloped
the entire structure. luckily no cry ol
fear came, though women's faces were
white and mems faces tense with
anxiety. Then came vivid flash oi
lightning and the booming report ol
thunder reached the anxious crowd.


Darker grew the murky air. Atlength
so great was the darkness that the news
writers were compelled to pause, unable
to see. Quickly followed rattling burst
of rain upon the roof. Almost instantly
stream Of water flowed down through
crack, directly upon the heads Of the
New York delegation. Umbrellas were
hoisted and the storm was ON.


Furious wind, quick thunder rolls and
rain dashes continued ten minutes. Nc
cry OF fear or dismay was uttered. Sud.
denly as the storm had come it passed
away, and light followed within the
great hall: The wall Of faces took on 9
look OF relief.

A Belfast (Me.) woman got indignant
the other day at the shabby appearance Of
the lawn about her house. After moving
down her husband with wrath, she was
soon on the lawn herself with the lawn
mower. Back and forth she pushed the
machine, while the sun beamed soft and
melting on the downtrodden woman and
everything else.


From a shady nook her husband timidly
watched her determined display. For an
hour, in which she must have travelled
dozen miles, she worked, but, sad to relate,
not a blade of grass bowed to her indignant
endeavors.


Finally her husband picked up courage
enough to address her:


Hadn't you better turn the machine
over, my dear?"


She did turn the machine over-into the
gutter-and swept into the house with a
look that kept her husband at a distance
for several days.-Lewiston Journal.
